speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN CENTRE FOR MANAGEMENT DEVELOPMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to introduce Bill C-148, a bill to establish the Canadian Centre for Management Development.
This bill embodies the principles first set out by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and reinforced by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) in announcing the establishment of the Centre in a speech to the public policy forum in Toronto, April 14, 1988. In that speech, the Hon. Don Mazankowski noted that:

August 25, 1988
Canadian Centre for Management Development Act
"The Centre's principal purpose will be to enhance public sector management capacities and to develop and promote a strong corporate culture in the federal Public Service. Our vision is a credible national, world-class centre of excellence in teaching and research into public sector management.
"The six objects of the Centre address the need for our senior managers to equip themselves with new knowledge, skills and managerial techniques consistent with the requirements of the rapidly changing government environment. Daily, senior managers face such challenges as improving productivity while exercising fiscal restraint, dismantling bureaucratic rules and procedures while adapting to increased managerial accountability."

Given the need to reduce public spending for the foreseeable future, Public Service managers are and will be expected to provide more services of a higher quality with fewer human and fiscal resources. We are proud of the quality of our public service, and I believe that in establishing this centre we are building our strength and building for tomorrow. All governments and the Canadian public will be better served by Public Service managers who are trained and equipped for the challenges of the future as well of those of today.

The objectives of the management training programs, courses, seminars and research conducted by the Centre, which are set out in the bill, are very important. 1 am sure they will be strongly supported by all Members of this House. Some of the most important themes include: encouraging pride and excellence in the management of the Public Service; fostering a sense of the purposes, values and traditions of the Public Service; providing the hard skills and knowledge to respond to change and manage government programs and services efficiently and effectively; encouraging the attraction of persons of high calibre to the Public Service, and support their growth and development; encouraging a greater awareness in Canada of issues related to public sector management and the process of governance and involving a broad range of individuals and institutions in the Centre's pursuit of excellence in public administration.
The Centre will be advised by an independent advisory council made up of outstanding Canadians from the Public Service, private sector and academic community.
This bill is designed to ensure that the Canadian Centre for Management Development, with the guidance of its advisory council and leadership of its principal, will have substantial independence in managing the intellectual aspects of its own affairs. Through this independence, the Centre is guaranteed the flexibility and opportunities to consult widely in the development of world-class management programs consistent with the requirements of a highly qualified Public Service.
[DOT] (M40)

The centre will be advised by an independent advisory council made up of outstanding Canadians from the Public Service, private sector, and academic community. The centre
will be located in the historic LaSalle Academy in the National Capital Region. In addition, the centre will continue to operate in Touraine, Quebec, and will operate programs through existing federal facilities in western and Atlantic Canada. The centre will consult with individuals, institutions, and organizations concerned with management training in all regions of Canada to ensure that its programs, courses, seminars, and research benefit from the diversity of specific regional requirements in all parts of Canada.

1 am confident that this Bill addresses the need for change in the way in which our senior public servants are prepared for management roles. 1 am also confident that all Members recognize the importance of a well-qualified professional management cadre in the Public Service. I hope that all Members can support this Bill and expedite its passage through all stages today in order that it may be sent to the Senate as quickly as possible.
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for this opportunity to introduce a piece of legislation that marks a turning point in the history of the Public Service of Canada. This Bill is an expression of the Government's commitment to the continued excellence of the Public Service and faith in the continuing contribution of the Public Service to the good governance of this country.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude by thanking the Opposition parties for agreeing to pass this Bill today.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I take part today, on behalf of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), in this debate on second reading of Bill C-148.
First, I would like to correct an error made by our friend opposite when he said that the school of advanced studies in Government administration, or Canadian Centre for Management Development, as it is called in the Bill, was initiated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). It is important to set the record straight and give to Caesar what is his due, Mr. Speaker, for it was the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier who first put forward this idea in 1974. So it should not be thought that the Prime Minister invented the wheel in this matter, as that is clearly not the case. Although we are grateful to the Government for having finally introduced the Bill at last, it must not be given the credit for the original idea. That would be a mistake, I think, and I am sure Canadians would not want to be misled, even if inadvertently.
Then, Mr. Speaker, on October 31, 1977, the Honourable Member for Ottawa-Vanier introduced in the House his Bill C-304. I have a copy of that Bill before me, and it attests to the fact that it was really and truly he who proposed this initiative. In 1977 my colleague moved two motions in the House for discussion of this matter, one on May 6 and the other on October 31, 1977. In 1981, he moved a new motion, which this time was debated in the House. Finally, in 1987, he once again had a motion put on the Order Paper to establish a national school of government administration.
August 25, 1988

So I hardly need to say, Mr. Speaker, that we of the Liberal Party are in complete agreement on this Bill, because it represents a Liberal initiative. We are proud of it, and we are happy to see that the present Government has adopted this good idea of my colleague's, the Honourable Member for Ottawa-Vanier.
The need for such a Centre is clear, since it arises in part from the study of the merit principle within the Public Service, known as the D'Avignon Report, which was launched by the Liberal government of the day.
1 shall keep my comments very brief, Mr. Speaker. I would be happy if in Committee of the Whole House we could discuss clause 4 and see, for example, how the whole matter of centralization of copyright and so forth will operate, under the Centre's direction. I would also like the Parliamentary Secretary to give us details about this matter, but I will not take up the House's time at this point. Perhaps it could be clarified in a few minutes' time, in Committee of the Whole.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like on behalf of my colleagues in the Liberal Party to express once again, to reiterate, our support for this initiative, an initiative that was first brought before this House, as I said just now, in 1974, by the Honourable Member for Ottawa-Vanier.

Mr. Speaker, I have had a chance to look at the Bill and to read some of the statements made by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazan-kowski) and by Jack Manion, a distinguished public servant who is the principal designate for the proposed Canadian centre for management studies. The New Democrats will support this Bill, but I must make a few comments on it. If we were in government we would perhaps do it a little differently than is being proposed by the Conservatives. Perhaps that is because they are Conservatives and we are not.
There are some general problems in terms of access to management positions in the Government of Canada which are not being resolved by the present Government and 1 believe they should be addressed by the centre for management studies. The question of interface and co-operation between the proposed centre and public administration programs across the country is one which needs to be addressed in a rather serious way. We are talking about a substantial new management education facility. There are probably a dozen programs in public administration in different universities across the country including Carleton University, Queen's, and York, of which I am a graduate. I am sure there are many others across the country.
Mr. Manion suggests that those centres of public administration have been devoted far too much to policy analysis and not really to public sector management. It seems to me that one of the priorities ought to be to try to work with various programs of public administration to get to the questions of
Canadian Centre for Management Development Act
management and not only to the questions of policy analysis, program evaluation, and that kind of thing.
The board of the centre has been announced. I am afraid I do not have the names before me. However, 1 suspect the list is short in terms of the number of women who have been appointed. I believe that one of the priorities for the centre should be to facilitate and accelerate the movement of women into management positions in the Government of Canada.
The recent announcement made by the President of the Treasury Board (Miss Carney) was more than disappointing. It suggested that by 1991 the representation of women in the management category of the Government of Canada stands to be increased by about 200 from 1987, up to 678. That is 50 a year, which is not very many. We know that most of those women are likely to be at the junior, rather than the senior management levels. They would be about 15 per cent of the employees in that category. That is not good enough, if there is a real commitment to equality and affirmative action by the government of the day. Certainly we hope to see that greatly improved.
The other area of preferred positions on which employment equity was meant to apply was in the scientific and professional areas, where the Government in fact anticipates not an increase but a reduction in the number of women in those positions by some 200 in the course of the next three or four years.
A number of the people who should be considered for management positions are now in bargaining unit positions.

Mr. Speaker, thank you for ignoring that irrelevant point of order.
The point 1 am making is that the centre for management development which is being set up and intends to be a centre for excellence has a specific role with respect to management in the Government of Canada. I believe one of those roles is to ensure that women managers and women intending to be managers should be facilitated and encouraged. One way to do that would be to ensure that there is a substantial number of women on the advisory board of the council of the centre in order that that priority is not forgotten.

August 25, 1988
Canadian Centre for Management Development Act
I would like to have seen representatives of the Public Service unions on the advisory board. 1 would like to have a commitment from the Government that that will be its intention, should it have a chance to form a government after the forthcoming election.
While it may be somewhat surprising to Mr. Manion, since the centre will be moving its activities to the vicinity of Parliament Hill, I believe there may be value in having some direct involvement of Members of Parliament who may be interested in some of the courses and work which is carried out in the centre.
When public servants' jobs bring them in close contact with the Hill, they learn a great deal. I know that when the work of Members of Parliament brings them in closer contact with the Public Service, they generally are struck with the capacity and responsibility carried by people in the Public Service.
Part of the ongoing commitment to excellence of the centre should include some access for Members of Parliament who may be interested in learning more about the problems and prospects for Public Service management. Perhaps some special courses might be designed that would bring students in the centres and Members of Parliament together. Perhaps courses could be designed which might be directed specifically at Members of Parliament and take into account the difficulties they have with not being able to focus on these matters just prior to elections and so on. It could help them to learn a bit more about the current thinking of management in the Government of Canada.
The principal elect, Mr. Manion, has already indicated his priorities and preferences. In an article in Dialogue he spoke about what he calls a big campaign to decentralize, deregulate, deburden and debureaucratize. He suggests that the centre will be heading in that particular direction.
I believe a great deal of thought must be given to the question of how to combine accountability with effective management in a public sector environment. Much thought should be given to ways of increasing access to information about what happens within Government. Some of the hierar-chal management structures which have been traditional in the Public Service must be broken down. The idea that a department can only talk to the public or to elected Members of Parliament through the elected minister at the top of the department is an outdated one. The suspicion, which unfortunately exists between departments and both the public and elected representatives of the public in Parliament, is a barrier which must be broken down.
Public Service managers should understand that they can be more open and, in turn, should be given an assurance that they will not be squashed by a superior or a minister for being more open. That is an attitude which leads to the present patterns of
secrecy, lack of knowledge and lack of understanding about what happens within the Public Service.
Mr. Manion has also spoken about the desire to continue to encourage a corporate culture in the senior leadership of the Government of Canada. I do not think people could have many problems with that.
He has spoken about trying to build a fairly homogenized group of managers. That causes me some difficulty because it suggests that a general management cadre is capable of going into all areas of government. I am not sure whether that is still the case as it was perhaps 10 or 20 years ago. I suspect that the policy of moving people from one management position to another at the senior level may be too generous. At the same time we constrain too tightly the ability of people in the more junior levels of government to broaden their experience by moving from one department to another. That is increasingly difficult and people are stuck into one pattern of career growth.
For example, a student who happens to join the Department of Fisheries and Oceans may be stuck in that Department all his or her life, with almost no chance of moving out. There are only a couple of departments, such as the Department of Finance, which provide entrees for people to go into other areas. It has been suggested that the centre will work with a case study approach. I believe that approach, along with the desire to have more cases written up and available, is valuable.
I want to conclude with a couple of suggestions that I hope the centre, in its research function and its dealing with people in the backrooms of politics and elected representatives, will take into consideration. One concerns the problem the present Government faced but did not solve particularly well. Due to the increasing complexity of government, even if the number of employees is not larger, the way a new government provides direction to the Public Service in implementing the programs and policies of that government and party is very difficult. The present Government put in chiefs of staff and increased very substantially the money that used to be paid to executive assistants to ministers under the Liberals in the hope that it would give greater clout to ministers' offices in order to ensure that there was a more effective means of translating into action what ministers in the government want. 1 am not sure whether that has been wholly successful.
According to the American model, after the forthcoming election, some 3,000 or 4,000 senior positions will be replaced, affecting the top levels of major U.S. government departments. That is not a very good model. We should look for a model which would provide means by which there could be effective political direction without compromising the need for professional management while at the same time being responsive to government.
August 25, 1988

Both Mr. Manion and 1 have been involved with the question of political rights. It is quite obvious that the senior Public Service and senior departments have interests of their own and must be acknowledged as having almost a political presence in the Government of Canada. That is a problem which at least has to be identified and which calls for some solution.
Let me conclude by expressing on behalf of many very hardworking public servants their resentment and concern over a decision that has been made by the Government. There is an elitism that is taking place in the Government of Canada in the differing treatment between the management employees and the rank and file. It is expressed in the fact that the Government has decided to give pay increases of between 8 per cent and 12 per cent to senior managers, deputy ministers and so on in the Government of Canada at a time when it has pay standards for other employees in the order of 3.5 per cent to 4 per cent per annum.
1 do not think that helps morale at all. There is a real sense of unfairness and injustice among people living in my constituency and in the constituencies of the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) and the Hon. Member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), people living in the capital region and elsewhere who are working for the Government of Canada because the Government decided to sock it to average civil servants at the same time it was giving raises of as much as $12,000, $13,000 or $15,000 to people earning over $100,000 in very senior management positions.
The Member for Ottawa-Carleton, who is going back to the private sector after this election, is about to leap to his feet to suggest that this is not very relevant. Perhaps it is not entirely in order with respect to this particular Bill, but I have been wanting to make this point for some time. I would hope as well that Mr. Manion, who I can see just behind him, would also be conscious of the fact that the perceived injustice is a very real one. After the tax bite is taken, those people working in average jobs in the Public Service are looking at a decline in their real incomes year after year, but the present Government has seen fit to give substantial increases to people in senior management categories. I think there is injustice and inequity there and I am sorry it occurs.
With those comments, I wish Mr. Manion well. If he wants me to lecture occasionally to his students at the centre, I will be happy to oblige. If he wants to offer some courses which would be available for Members of Parliament to participate in, and I am not in Government, I would be happy to try to take part.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Claudy Mailly (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: CANADIAN CENTRE FOR MANAGEMENT DEVELOPMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think this is a time for political partisanship, and I am sorry to see that is indeed what is happening.
I am delighted to see this Bill tabled during my Government's mandate, because it comes as the culmination of the
Canadian Centre for Management Development Act
work done by many Members and by the D'Avignon Commission.
As was pointed out by the Hon. Member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell (Mr.Boudria), the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) worked very hard for this happy ending. Another Member of this House also worked very hard toward the same goal, and I am referring to the late Walter Baker who, as a Member and later as Minister, showed a keen interest in the cause of professionalism and especially the merit principle in the Public Service.
We are very proud of the Public Service of Canada, which consists of men and women who daily demonstrate how professionals can and should behave in some very difficult situations where they must provide solutions that are both objective and helpful to a Government that is trying to solve some very complex problems.
I would like to take this opportunity on second reading to say that this morning, I met John Manion, the Director of the new Centre for which the enabling legislation was introduced today, and he gave me the assurance that contrary to rumors and also to certain representations that were made to me by public servants involved in this area, the Centre for Executive Development in Touraine, which was mentioned by the Parliamentary Secrertary in his speech, will not be closed. In fact, it will be a focal point in the centre for excellence we are creating officially today. Furthermore, Mr. Manion would like to see the Centre expanded to respond to the needs and expectations expressed in this Bill.
The public servants who made their representations and the journalists who said that the Centre would be closed, may rest assured that will not be the case. The Centre will continue to function. Its purpose has been confirmed, and I am delighted because it happens to be in my riding, and not just because it is physically present, but because, as you know, Mr. Speaker, we have trouble convincing certain people in politics that the Quebec side of the National Capital is an integral part of the National Capital. Later today, we will have the privilege of considering the NCC bill, which will once again confirm the bilingual and bi-cultural calling of our National Capital.
Again, I am delighted the Centre is in my riding and that, in its own way, it reflects the role played by the Quebec side in the National Capital region and in the work done by the Canadian Government in this country.

subtopic: CANADIAN CENTRE FOR MANAGEMENT DEVELOPMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to add a few comments as well during debate on this very important Bill. At this very moment there is a seminar taking place at the Chateau Laurier by the Public Policy Forum, an organization based here in Ottawa. It is focusing on the actual future management practices of the centre itself. The Deputy Secretary to the Cabinet, and designated principal of the future Centre, and, I should add, a constituent of mine, spoke there yesterday and outlined some of the priorities he would like to see the management centre pursue. I would like to just give some brief comments about what he said.

August 25, 1988
Canadian Centre for Management Development Act
I think he focused very briefly on the fact that the time has now come for the need to develop a set of programs and find the best people to administer them in the management centre. It is important to train our Public Service managers with new techniques and skills to allow them to deal with, as he said humorously yesterday, the "unexpected" which seems to be happening more and more frequently in our daily lives in dealing with public matters.
He talked about the importance of learning from other institutions, particularly those in the United States and the United Kingdom. Yesterday as well at the Centre, Dr. Loretta Flanders, who is the special assistant to the director of the Office of Executive Personnel Management, Office of Personnel Management, Government of the United States, focused on what she called a Framework for Management Excellence: The American Experience. The new centre in Canada will hope to benefit from these practices which have been going on in the United States and Great Britain over the last eight or ten years. One thing the centre can and should do is help managers relate more closely to the role of Members of Parliament, with enhanced reform in Parliament and a greater role for us to play in the legislative practice and creation of public policy.
Dealing with interest groups will be a very important aspect of the management training centre as well as the results of the impact of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which we are now seeing as having wide repercussions throughout not only public, but private life. Indeed, one could add the aftermath of the introduction of the free trade agreement which will have significant impact on the operations of so many government Departments.
The centre will hopefully publish the results of its work and work very closely with private sector experiences in having seminars and bringing in researchers from the private sector to allow our public servant managers to benefit from the great amount of experience there is in the private sector. The need for this Bill is important. It is timely and will give the centre what has been called its intellectual independence. It will lead,
I hope, to a better management and therefore a much stronger Public Service of Canada. It will ultimately benefit all Canadians.

I am very proud to support the creation of the Canadian Centre for Management Development.

The Bill is timely. It is important. It will help our Public Service immensely to train our managers to be better managers, and we look forward to the passage of this Bill in all stages today.

subtopic: CANADIAN CENTRE FOR MANAGEMENT DEVELOPMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief in my remarks in welcoming this initiative. I congratulate the Government on taking an initiative which is long overdue.
We have a good Public Service in Canada. It has been said for years that it is one of the best in the world. I certainly agree with that. I am proud to have been a member of the Public Service. I am proud to represent tens of thousands of public servants in the House of Commons of Canada. However, I recognize that there is a need for a management centre such as that which will be created in this Bill today.
I refer to some of the objects found in Clause 4 of the Bill, particularly subclause (a) which states:
"(a) to encourage pride and excellence in the management of the Public Service and to foster among its managers a sense of the purposes, values and traditions of the Public Service".
I have some sense as a former public servant and a resident of this community of those traditions. My great grandfather was a public servant in Ottawa. I have on my wall in my Parliament Hill office a framed copy of a certificate, certifying that he passed the civil service examination in 1883.
We have a long tradition of very fine individuals who have leadership roles in the Public Service of Canada. I refer to people such as Bob Bryce, Gordon Robertson, O. D. Skelton and Dr. John Deutsch, former inhabitants of my university at Queens in Kingston who were very much a part of the relationship between the university sector and the federal Public Service. This is an important initiative. It is very much in the tradition of that excellence.
I wish to be bold enough to make one recommendation, if I may, on the curriculum that might be considered in the many courses that will be offered at the management centre. I make it as a former officer of the Department of Justice, if I may suggest it to the principal designate, Jack Manion, who I wish well in his new duties. I refer to the importance of ensuring that Public Service managers are made aware of and have an opportunity to learn more about the legal process and the legal nature of decision-making in the federal Public Service. This is becoming a complex matter. It always really has been when one considers statutes such as the Financial Administration Act and the many onerous responsibilities that are placed upon Public Service managers under that Act, as well as under the Public Service Employment Act and so many others.
In light of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the increasing role of private Members of Parliament, for example, under parliamentary reform, it is important that Public Service managers focus on issues such as the legal aspects of the structure of government and the legal aspects of government operations in terms of the policy process, the program process, its administrative and, certainly, the financial control process.
August 25, 1988

The whole notion of law reform, institutional and procedural reform and constitutional reform are all matters that would prudently be the subject matter of courses at the management centre.
Having made that brief suggestion, may I once again congratulate the Government on this important and historic initiative. I wish all Public Service managers who will be enrolled from time to time at courses at the centre the very best.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stewart Mclnnes (Minister of Public Works) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
speechtext:
that Bill C-153, an Act to amend the National Capital Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this Bill allows the Government to carry through on a promise which was made during the Speech from the Throne on October 1.
Must you put it that way?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
speechtext:
Thank you, Hon. Member. We are trying to crystalize and focus our attention more formally on activities carried out by the NCC, which indeed have been part of their unofficial mandate for a long period of time. Perhaps the mandate as expressed in the Bill, in the legislation now existing, is too restrictive, too concerned with bricks and mortar. We want to amplify and embellish and expand the powers of the NCC to undertake the promotion, as it has done so very well during the past number of years, with respect to giving more focus and new direction on Ottawa and the National Capital Region, as Canada's meeting place, to ensure that it communicates Canada to Canadians and to safeguard and preserve the capital. So the amendments are of a very simple nature and they are necessary for the efficient functioning of the NCC.
There are several proposals with respect to land use changes, demolitions, and land sales, and to give it authority concerning these particular matters it will prevent the demolition of heritage buildings, the inappropriate use of federal lands and will better provide tools to realize the principles of the federal land use plan to the benefit of both the NCR and the longterm interest of all Canadians.
With the passage of this legislation, this Government will be seen as being the first Government to live up to its commitment of strengthening the symbolic significance of the capital.
Yes. Sure.
When are we going to become a province?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
speechtext:
I suggest that this Bill will enable the NCC
to improve its co-operation with other levels of government in
the capital, by providing quick responses to the giving of
August 25, 1988

easements and co-ordinating the effort with respect to all matters involving land owned by the Government in the NCR.
I want to thank Members, in anticipation of their positions today, who have been very co-operative in allowing us to advance this Bill which 1 think is in the national interest.

Mr. Speaker, the first thing that 1 would like to do today is to offer my words of congratulations to the Minister, who became a father only a few days ago. I am sure that I speak on behalf of all of my colleagues in offering the Minister and Mrs. Mclnnes my very best words of congratulations, which I sent to him in writing a few days ago.
I should correct the Minister when he refers to Bill C-153 and his Government being the first Government to improve the symbolic significance of the National Capital Region. Far be it from me to try to correct the Minister, but let me try anyway to remind the Minister that in 1899 the federal Government created the Ottawa Improvement Commission. In 1913, the then Borden Government established the Federal Plan Commission. In 1927, the Government established the Federal District Commission. In 1945, under the Federal District Commission Act, Mr. Greber, the noted French planner, was appointed to prepare the Greber Plan. In 1949, the first Master Plan of the National Capital Region was commissioned in the House of Commons. In 1951 that plan was tabled in Parliament. In 1956, a joint parliamentary committee endorsed the continued implementation of the plan. In 1969 the First Ministers endorsed the Greber plan as a vision for a unified capital, extending it across both sides of the Ottawa River.
Do you know where I got that information, Mr. Speaker?
From the NCC.
From the Minister's briefing notes that were supplied to us.
Oh, oh!

I know the Minister has come back from his constituency lately for obvious reasons, but I remind him that he has perhaps overstated somewhat the involvement of his Government in terms of the National Capital Region.
I have here a copy of the National Capital Region report which was the work of a committee of this House for two years, which report was tabled in this House in 1976. The Minister and his Government certainly have not re-invented the wheel in terms of commitment to the National Capital Region. Indeed, there have been 85 years of planning, according to the Minister's own briefing notes, in the National Capital Region by the National Capital Commission and predecessor organizations. That is some of the history of the National Capital Commission and the development of that Commission and its predecessors in the development of our area.
National Capital Act
I am sure that I speak on behalf of all Members of the House when I say that through the organization we now know of as the NCC this city is far more beautiful than it otherwise would have been. The National Capital Commission is upon occasion everyone's favorite whipping boy, including mine when it does something that I dislike. I usually raise the matter when I dislike what it does, but I also raise matters publicly when I like what it does. Sometimes the subjects are controversial. I remember last year the National Capital Commission came up with the idea that we should have coloured pavement in front of Parliament and other buildings such as exists in Boston and in London, England in front of Buckingham Palace. That red pavement was not particularly well liked by some Government back-benchers and they convinced the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) to kibosh to the plan.
Which one?
The same Deputy Prime Minister we have now.
Which back-benchers?

I could name them individually if the Member wants me to but I will avoid that embarrassment for the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) who like myself liked the idea proposed at that time by the National Capital Commission. I said on the floor of this House that I thought the plan should proceed. I still think it should proceed because I think it is a good idea. 1 say to the Member from Winnipeg-undoubtedly he has travelled and seen that kind of decoration in front of other legislative buildings and in other downtown areas-it is a good idea into which a lot of thought went but that plan was scuttled.
On behalf of my Party, I want to speak in favour of the Bill. There are a few questions I will want to ask in Committee of the Whole. I hope the Minister will have the officials available to us to answer questions, particularly as to the authority the NCC will have over private lands under the Bill. I am particularly concerned about that because in no way do I want to interfere with the powers that municipalities have at the present time.
I for one am pleased that we are recognizing in statute what the NCC is doing already in terms of its role in the programming area. I think of Winterlude, the very successful winter carnival that we have in Ottawa, which 1 believe is now the second-largest winter carnival in the country. That is a tremendous endeavour. Our Canada Day celebrations are something of which all Canadians are proud. Tourists come here not only from our country but from around the world and have remarked about the marvellous job done in organizing the Canada Day celebrations. Those celebrations are in part the responsibility of the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard), but the NCC, of course, plays a leading role in the organization of the activities.

August 25, 1988
National Capital Act
The NCC has also provided such things as bicycle paths and set up skating on the canal, et cetera. 1 want to take this occasion to say that I hope the winter and summer outdoor activities continue to be offered on a no-charge basis in the National Capital Region, whether for local people or for people coming from the Minister's riding in Halifax. The last thing people want to be doing after paying considerable money to travel to our capital is to go through a toll booth on the Rideau Canal. I hope that never happens, but it is an idea brought to our attention.
1 congratulate the Chairman of the National Capital Commission. She brings a lot of thought provoking ideas to us, some of which I disagree with but the majority 1 do agree with. It does not matter that 1 disagree with them from time to time. The Chairman is thought-provoking in that she brings forth matters for public discussion and has the fortitude to do so. That is good in its own way because it causes us to pause and reflect on various ideas.
The Government in the Throne Speech of September, 1986, said it would bring this Bill forward. We are glad to see, nearly two years later, that the Government has done so. On behalf of my Party, as the Official Opposition spokesman, I agreed that the Bill should proceed forthwith.
1 want to take a few moments though to discuss something about the National Capital Commission that involves my constituency and invite the Minister in that regard to pay very close attention. I think that the boundaries of the National Capital Commission are not appropriately divided right now and 1 am looking for the Minister's co-operation. Presently the National Capital designated region under the schedule of the Act extends some 70 or 80 kilometres westward from the Parliament Buildings, which I believe is the focus of the whole area. Conversely, if you were to go in an easterly direction toward my constituency, the National Capital Region extends only some 20 or 25 kilometres. 1 do not feel that is appropriate. Land, particularly the islands on the Ottawa River east of Cumberland, and land in the area of Rockland, Clarence and Plantaganet should be protected. There is no better tool as far as I am concerned than the National Capital Commission to preserve and protect those lands east of the city in a manner consistent with the protection given on the western side of the city.
I have suggested to the National Capital Commission that that should be done. The Minister is probably aware that I have raised this publicly as something I would support. I wish I could take credit for the idea myself, Mr. Speaker, but it is not mine. The idea was brought to my attention by the Mayor of Rockland, His Worship Jean-Marc Lalonde, who suggested extending the National Capital Region eastward.
We are presently having meetings. I thank the Minister and the Chairman of the National Capital Commission for providing the staff to brief the local mayors on the advantages of having the area designated in terms of the National Capital Region, and we are having meetings with the other local
mayors in the vicinity to obtain their concurrence for this kind of initiative. With this concurrence, which I hope will come shortly, 1 would then like to propose a Private Member's Bill to this House to change the boundaries of the National Capital Region. 1 hope the Government will give the same kind of cooperation to that as we are giving today to the Government's own Bill.
I want to speak to a few items in the Bill. 1 agree with the part of the Bill that suggests the head office of the National Capital Commission could be located in an area other than Ottawa. All parts of the national capital district should be treated equally, whether those parts are Gatineau, Hull, Orleans or Carp. They are all equal parts of the national capital area, and if the NCC wants to have an office located in one part rather than the other, that should be permitted. Mr. Speaker, I will support this Bill and my Party supports it. As a Member from the National Capital Region, 1 support the Bill because its major purpose is to put into legislation in the National Capital Act effectively what the National Capital Commission has been doing increasingly over the past few years. Rather than
August 25, 1988

dealing just with hard services and with putting into place parkways and beautifying the National Capital Region, the NCC is increasingly promoting various kinds of public activities and events which are worthy of a national capital and which enable Canadians from this area and from across Canada to sense a celebration of a country when they are here in the national capital or when they see events in the national capital via the media.
The existing Section 10 of the National Capital Act provides that most of the powers that are given to the Commission are related to the physical appearance of the National Capital Region. According to that section, the Commission has the power to acquire and administer property, to lease or dispose of property, to build parks and squares, highways and parkways, bridges and buildings and other works, to improve its own property or other property managed by government departments, to co-operate with local municipalities or authorities to improve or develop or to maintain property and to construct places of entertainment, amusement, recreation or refreshment upon property owned by the Commission. It is all related to property.
1 have been a resident of the Ottawa area for some 22 years, and I know there is no question that the National Capital Commission has done an excellent job in implementing the dream of various planners, including the dream of the Greber Commission which was held just after the war and has given us the parkways along the canal. It has opened up the canal in the downtown core between Sandy Hill and Centretown where there used to be train traffic to the Union Station. It has given us the parkways along the Ottawa River and now the new parkway out toward the aviation museum. It has given us the development of the Gatineau and the rest of it. However, a country is people and a capital is about people. That is why the National Capital Commission's efforts have been redirected.
There has been a slowing down of the emphasis on the physical appearance of the national capital and from time to time, the Commission has been putting extra pressure on the local municipalities, suggesting that they should not expect to get all parks and recreation projects developed for them by the National Capital Commission. Sometimes the NCC acted a bit like a sugar daddy to local municipalities, and having once been an alderman in the City of Ottawa, I feel that that is a perfectly natural reaction. Sometimes the NCC is forced to say no.
The Bill proposes that the objects and purposes of the Commission be expanded to allow the Commission to organize or to sponsor or to promote public activities in events in the National Capital Region that will enrich the cultural and social fabric of Canada, taking into account the federal and bilingual character of Canada and the heritage of the people of Canada. That sounds like some of the language that touches all bases in the Constitution of Canada, but I suppose that also reflects the nature of the country.
National Capital Act

If the National Gallery, in its wonderful new premises, proposes to put on a blockbuster exhibition next summer, that presumably would be an activity or event, but would it be related to the National Capital Region. Would the NCC have the right to co-ordinate that particular program or not? I do not know. I will not move an amendment to the clause because I am prepared to take this on faith. I think its major purpose is to put into legislation enough power so that the NCC can do what it has been doing, such things as co-ordinating the Destination '88 tourism program, pulling together the two regional municipalities, the private sector and the tourist industry in order to make the region an increasingly important place for Canadians and for foreigners to put on their itineraries when they decide to travel to this part of the country.

They really like our city, and one of the reasons they like our city is because of its appearance. Another is because of the extraordinary variety of activities that take place.
We have come to the middle of August, and some of my friends are saying that they are almost festivalled out by now because of the number of festivals and public events which have taken place. Mr. Speaker, I am particularly pleased with Clause 2 of the Bill. This clause repeals Section 5 of the Act that created the National Capital Commission and reads as follows:
"5. (1) The head office of the Commission shall be in the National Capital
Region.
(2) The Commission shall meet at least three times a year in the National

That may seem very simple, Mr. Speaker, but when you see what it replaces, you realize how big this change is. Previously, the Act said: "The Commission shall meet at least three times a year in the city of Ottawa, and it may meet at such other times in the National Capital Region as the Commission deems necessary."
So, Mr. Speaker, here in this Bill, we officially confirm that the National Capital Region is not just the City of Ottawa. This is a very important point, because, Mr. Speaker, the 1867 Statute which made Ottawa the capital of Canada simply mentioned Ottawa, which in 1867 meant about a dozen streets on the Ontario side of the capital.
This statute was not amended. I myself tried to present a Private Member's Bill to say that the seat of the Government of Canada is the National Capital Region, in order to confirm the fact that our capital is on both sides of the Ottawa River and naturally takes in the Quebec part. Unfortunately, or fortunately, I was made a Parliamentary Secretary and I could not pursue this Bill.
So the Bill before us goes in the same direction. Just now, my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell	(Mr. Boudria) objected that the Minister said it was the first time that a Government confirmed the symbolic role of the NCC. But the Minister was absolutely right. It is the first time that the NCC's symbolic role on both sides of the Ottawa River has been confirmed; it confirms for the first time that the capital is not only Ottawa, a few streets in Ottawa, but the region, which includes the Quebec side.

What we are talking about here is nation building, as our very beloved Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) often says. We have an anglophone Minister from Nova Scotia and a chairman of the Commission, who is an anglophone from the Ontario side of our capital, who have understood the aspirations of French-speaking people and how important this is, not only symbolically, that this is enshrined in law that the capital of our country is in the region which covers both sides of the Ottawa River, including the Quebec side where the majority of the people are French speaking. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I say that the geography is not in stone. We are prepared to entertain discussions with the Hon. Member and any constituency. I would invite him to do that. I will not make any commitments but we will certainly entertain dialogue.

Mr. Chairman, 1 have listened with interest to the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. I want to caution the Hon. Member. I come from the west coast. Looking at the National Capital and the National Capital Region, I am proud of our capital. I do not want the capital region to grow in size. It is a very costly venture as it is. Members here are trying judicially to look after what taxpayers' money is spent on. Just how large a region do we need? That is a debatable point.
1 caution the Hon. Member not to tell his people at home that their area will be put into the National Capital Region so that suddenly the NCC will start looking after a great deal of his riding. Coming from British Columbia, 1 am not sure I want to see the national capital grow too much larger than the region it already occupies.

Mr. Chairman, 1 wish to speak on this particular clause in order to avoid speaking on third reading, perhaps in response to the Hon. Member as well as to the Minister.
1 thank the Minister for his response, which provides me with cautious optimism. 1 want to indicate to the Hon. Member who has expressed concern that I as well share his concern. 1 appreciate the position which he brings forward.
What 1 am asking is that the National Capital Region be permitted to exist in an equal distance east of Ottawa as it does west of Ottawa. We are not asking for anything to be changed that is not consistent with the present policy. Surely, if it warrants reserving an area of protection some 50 miles on one side of the city then it should be consistent on the other side. That is merely what I was stating today.
National Capital Act
The Hon. Member should realize that just because an area is designated by the National Capital Commission, it does not necessarily mean that the Commission will have to spend funds on it. We know that the NCC only has authority over lands that it owns and not over other lands. If the owner of one of the islands which 1 mentioned earlier in the Ottawa River wanted to give the land to the National Capital Commission, the NCC could not accept it because it is not within that territory, something which I believe it should be. Even if the NCC could get the land for nothing it could not accept it. That is why I am looking for those changes.
With those remarks I will conclude by adding the following. My colleague from Ottawa-Vanier has suggested to the National Capital Commission in the area of programs for some time that the NCC should develop a system of what he calls visitors' passports which would permit a visitor from out of town coming to the city to buy at a discount rate a ticket to the National Arts Centre, the National Gallery and the Museum of Civilization, and so on. By buying the tickets all together, one would receive a discount. Also, this would be in the form of a passport book which could be stamped as the person visits the facilities and brought back home as a souvenir. I think that the idea is novel. It is an interesting one. I want to take this opportunity to restate it and invite the NCC to look at the proposal suggested by my colleague. 1 do not necessarily need a response to it immediately. However, I want to restate it for the benefit of the House.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I made a mistake when I spoke earlier. 1 mentioned that the NCC was founded in 1968. It has been beavering away since 1958. I would like that error corrected since I might not be here this afternoon when the "blues" come around.
I also wish to say to the Minister that I appreciate the work that the NCC is doing in my area. However, I would like to underline the fact that perhaps the NCC has been intervening on the Quebec side only recently, in the last 10 years, and that we in the Municipality of Gatineau, which is the main city in my riding, are a little bit worried about the 10-year plan which has been introduced by the NCC. There does not seem to be too much that the NCC will be doing in our territory. I would like the Minister to again take a look at that plan to ensure that we are not blocked from development for the next 10 years because it is not in that 10-year plan. It is very important for the citizens in my area to feel that they are indeed part of the National Capital Region, which they are.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could just ask one final question of the Minister which I omitted to ask him earlier. It pertains to the change in the Bill with regard to the Financial Administration Act whereby the NCC is looking for a mandate so that it would not be required to go to Treasury Board when approving contracts. We did that in a clause that is already accepted but under the general heading of the title

August 25, 1988
clause. Of course, I think you would find, Mr. Chairman, that the question would be in order nevertheless. I want to be assured that in fact we will be having rules and regulations under the Financial Administration Act until such time as a completely different set of rules is established for the NCC which would permit it to entertain the construction of a piece of roadway, for instance, and not have to go to Treasury Board, which is a sometimes awkward and lengthy process in order to complete the construction of a project, say, before winter comes. 1 understand that that is a problem now. 1 want to be assured that the rules will be in effect until the new rules are designed for the NCC in such a way so as to preserve the tendering process and so on of the Government.
1 also want to make sure that the new rules that are adopted by the National Capital Commission will be done in such a manner so as to preserve in the long term the tendering process while assuring that something speedier is there than the present rules which I recognize are cumbersome.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I give the assurance to the Hon. Member that we are making this Crown corporation perform as all other Crown corporations perform. A set of rules and a tendering process like other Crown corporations will be put in place.

Title agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

It being after 1 p.m., I do now leave the chair until 2 p.m. this day.
At 1.40 p.m. the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, the grave accident at Saint-Basile-le-Grand points to the urgent necessity of accelerating research to render PCBs harmless by way of a neutralizing process.
Across Canada there are hundreds, perhaps thousands of locations where PCBs are stored, posing a potential risk to the population. It becomes, therefore, imperative to intensify research so as to arrive very soon at a technological breakthrough that would greatly benefit Canadians.
Unfortunately, this Government weakened the research capability of the National Research Council when in November, 1984, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) cut the NRC
budget by over $60 million. Once again we call on the Government to reverse that decision and provide the NRC with the funds necessary for accelerated research on ways and means to neutralize PCBs. This is a matter of urgent public interest.

Mr. Speaker, the monthly rents being charged civil servants and the RCMP who live in Government owned houses in Banff National Park are excessive. A three-bedroom single family detached home in Banff rents for $800 to $1,100, while a similar home in Jasper National Park is $300 lower, and in other national parks the rents are up to $600 lower.
When compared with monthly rents in similar Alberta towns Banff is higher by more than $400. In addition, Parks Canada has been reluctant to set aside areas for single family homes and so renters have no choice. No wonder the Banff civil servants are enraged. I ask the President of the Treasury Board (Miss Carney) to lower the Banff rates so they are, at least, at the same level as rents charged in Jasper. When Government is a landlord it should be an example of fairness and should never act as an oppressive tyrant.

maintopic: UNNECESSARY VIOLENCE IN NATIONAL HOCKEY LEAGUE
UNNECESSARY VIOLENCE IN NATIONAL HOCKEY LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a few short weeks from now hundreds of thousands of Canadian young people from coast to coast will be getting ready for another season of amateur hockey. Many will spend long hours on the hockey rinks practising and honing their skills, and dreaming of one day playing in the National Hockey League.
Unfortunately, the NHL continues to turn a blind eye to unnecessary violence that all too often rears its ugly head. The inevitable result was what we witnessed yesterday-the spectacle of a handcuffed Dino Ciccarelli being led out of a courtroom and into a jail, all as a result of an unnecessary assault during a hockey game last season.
Hockey is a tough, rugged game that combines skill, strength, speed, and determination. But hockey is not a game for goons or a game where unnecessary violence should be tolerated at any level-and that includes the NHL.
August 25, 1988

Hockey is Canada's greatest contribution to the world of international sport. Hockey is our game, a Canadian game, and we should not let ugly, squalid scenes of blood and violence make it less than what it is-one of the world's greatest sports.
Perhaps the federal Government could help by developing an anti-violence poster, comparing Ciccarelli in handcuffs on one hand with the non-violent superstar Wayne Gretzky on the other, and posting it in the arenas of this land.

subtopic: WAREHOUSING SITES FOR PCBS IN ABITIBI-TEMISCAMINGUE
WAREHOUSING SITES FOR PCBS IN ABITIBI-TEMISCAMINGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no one in Quebec wanted the PCB disposal plant. What is dangerous in other places will also be dangerous where we live, in Abitibi.
The greatest concentration of PCBs is in Montreal and on the banks of the St. Lawrence, where the greatest concentration of population is too. It is very costly to remove the danger from these people by choosing Abitibi-Temiscamingue as a dump site. What will happen to us?
Bringing PCBs to Senneterre is only one step. Once they are all disposed of, other toxic wastes will follow. Opening the door to PCBs means opening the door to all toxic wastes. The region is big and we are few. However, we are very much alive and we love our environment. It is unacceptable for the Government of Quebec to use us as the garbage dump of North America.
I would like to quote (Quebec Environment) Minister Lincoln: "The issue of PCBs is very emotional; I do not judge these people in Senneterre. If there were a dump in Beacons-field tomorrow, perhaps I would react the same way."
Mr. Speaker, no PCBs in Abitibi-Temiscamingue!

Mr. Speaker, is there no low to which our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will not stoop in his attempt to keep quiet on issues of pressing national importance? I would like to read into the record a statement made by his former press aide, Michel Gratton.
When Mr. Gratton decided that he was going to write a book, no less than the Prime Minister went after him in a desperate attempt to try to stop him from telling the truth. "They got to me emotionally, using people I like to make me feel guilty. First they tried to stop me from writing the book, and when that did not work they tried to rattle me so I would
be nicer. When that didn't work, they spread rumours about my personal life. All this comes from Mulroney himself'.
That is is not a statement of a Liberal Member or an opposition Member. That is a statement of the former press aide to the Prime Minister. My mother always said, "You are judged by the company that you keep". I think that the reason that the Prime Minister is in the mess that he is in today is because dirt starts from the top down.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have listened carefully to the Hon. Member's statement, and I just want to remind Members that statements are not meant for personal attacks on other Hon. Members. I have accepted the statement, but 1 just wanted to mention that.

Mr. Speaker, we were glad to learn yesterday that the Government of Quebec is extending the moratorium on the Montreal-Saint-Hilaire suburban train until June 1989. However, we are sorry about two things in this matter: first, the complete absence of the Conservative Government in the search for a solution to the suburban transportation problem; second, the fact that the small municipalities in this region will have to cover a deficit that CN rejects. The reason there is a deficit, Mr. Speaker, is that CN and the federal Transport Minister never invested in improving suburban passenger service in this region. Again, Mr. Speaker, we are pleased with the initiative taken by the provincial Government and the municipalities to save their suburban trains, but we also deplore the absence of the federal Government, which should also contribute to the development of suburban train transportation in all regions of the country.

Mr. Speaker, formal negotiations aimed at bringing about a peaceful settlement in Cyprus will resume at long last on September 15, after some three and a half years of interruption.
The key issues in these negotiations will be the guarantee of minority rights and the possible establishment of a federal system of government.

August 25, 1988
Canada has maintained a peacekeeping force on Cyprus since 1963. We have an international reputation as a peace negotiator. We have experience with both minority rights guarantees and with a federal system of government.
Because of this I would urge our Government to take and to play an active role in these Cyprus peace negotiations.

Mr. Speaker, there are one and a half million Canadians of Italian origin living among us. They speak one of the most beautiful languages in the world. It is also one of the simplest languages of the world. It is very easy to pronounce for French and English speakers, and yet, in general, their fellow Canadians make very little effort to pronounce Italian names as they are pronounced by the people who hold those names.
The rules are so simple that they can be learned in less than a minute, and yet many Italian Canadian families are changing their own pronunciation of their names to correspond with the way that their fellow Canadians wrongfully pronounce them.
The rules are simple. Final e is pronounced, ch is pronounced like a k, c followed by e or i is pronounced like ch, and g followed by e or i is pronounced like j. What could be simpler?
Let us stop murdering the Italian language when we use these names, and start pronouncing them properly.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: CITY OF LACHINE-UNVEILING OF MONUMENT COMMEMORATING RENE LEVESQUE
CITY OF LACHINE-UNVEILING OF MONUMENT COMMEMORATING RENE LEVESQUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to add my most cordial greetings to all those who attended the unveiling of a monument by Robert Roussil in memory of Rene Levesque in Lachine on Monday evening.
As our Prime Minister wrote in his congratulatory message:
"Robert Roussil has created a strong, original work which not only reveals the talent of a great artist but also well expresses his deep understanding and admiration for Rene Levesque.
Whether or not one agrees with the ideal that guided Rene Levesque's commitment, he was one of that province's great political personalities for all Quebecers."
The presence of thousands of residents of Lachine at the unveiling shows attachment and recognition for this great democrat.
On behalf of all, I wish to congratulate Mayor Guy Descary, the members of his Council and the citizens of Lachine for this initiative.

subtopic: POSITION OF CANADIAN MEDICAL ASSOCIATION PRESIDENT
POSITION OF CANADIAN MEDICAL ASSOCIATION PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we agree with the President of the Canadian Medical Association that the emergence of a two-tier medical system, which favours the rich, and the lack of recognition of nurses are two serious problems facing Canada's medical system. We do not share his solutions. User-fees would undermine one of the best health care systems in the world, which must be accessible regardless of incomes.
With the rapidly growing aging population we must give much greater priority to community support, rather than costly institutionalization, and to preventive measures that promote health rather than having an obsession with expensive high technologies.
Despite the Health Minister's declared policy, only about 10 per cent of our health dollar goes into community health services and health promotion. The federal Government's overall contribution to health care has been reduced by $5.6 billion over the past five years.
Nurses must be recognized with decent pay and not privatized as in Alberta. Services of all health care practitioners should be covered directly under medicare. Governments must develop community health clinics with flexible outreach services.
We urge the federal Government to restore 50 per cent funding provided that provinces agree to much greater emphasis on prevention and health promotion.

subtopic: CALL FOR CHANGE TO OUTDATED REGULATION
CALL FOR CHANGE TO OUTDATED REGULATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to current registered retirement savings plan regulations we should all be dead by age 90, or if we are hardy enough to live that long we should be able to live without any money.
August 25, 1988

At age 71 an RRSP can be converted into a registered retirement income fund but the user must take out all the money by the age of 90. That may have been all right when the regulations were written, but now more and more Canadians are living into their nineties and the question arises what are they going to live on unless this outdated regulation is changed?
They cannot all be like my mother-in-law, Mr. Speaker, who is alive and well at age 93 and is still winning money at cards three nights a week.

Mr. Speaker, in June Callwood's column which appeared in The Globe and Mail yesterday she reported on the tragic plight of Elena Keis, a desperate, frightened woman living in Leningrad who applied for permission to emigrate to Israel eight years ago. Time is running out.
On September 9, her only son becomes 18 years old and will be conscripted into the Soviet Army. Elena Keis has been adopted by the Jewish community of Toronto. Michael Dukakis and his wife sent a cable recently to Mr. Gorbachev urging him to approve her application to leave.
Her mother, father, and older sister were permitted to leave the Soviet Union. She and her husband have not worked in sensitive jobs for more than five years. In this last year her physical and mental health has deteriorated drastically.
I am certain that all Members of Parliament will join with me when I urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to make representations to Mr. Gorbachev on Elena Keis' behalf.

Mr. Speaker, the Ontario Federation of Agriculture recently endorsed the Government's tax reform package as it relates to farmers.
Under tax reform farmers will still be able to use cash accounting rather than accrual accounting. Moreover, when it sorts people out for tax purposes the Government will not use either the profit test, to distinguish between farmers and nonfarmers, or the gross revenue test, to distinguish between fulltime and part-time farmers. Part-time farmers will now be able to claim farm losses of up to $8,750 against their other income. Full-time farmers will be able to claim all of their farm losses against other income.
The Government will also extend the flexible livestock inventory provision to all commodities, which will enable farmers to average their income over a number of years.
The Ontario Federation of Agriculture's endorsement of tax reform indicates how this Government achieves just and equitable results through consultation with those who will be affected by laws it contemplates making.

Mr. Speaker, three weeks ago the new FM station CHXL in Brockville began transmitting, and complaints regarding interference with telephones, TV reception, and other radio station reception have been flooding into my office.
I have called upon the Department of Communications to work closely with the broadcaster to resolve these complaints quickly and to bring about a solution to the problem.
In addition, area residents can now no longer receive the CBC signal from Kingston or Ottawa. CBC for 12 years has had a licence to transmit from its Maitland tower but because of technical difficulties has not fulfilled its responsibilities. As repeated strong representations have resulted in no action taken by the CBC, I therefore call upon the CBC to stop dragging its feet and meet its obligations immediately. If not, CRTC should revoke its licence.

Mr. Speaker, earlier today I had the honour of presenting a report entitled Nuclear Energy: Unmasking the Mystery.
This report has 14 recommendations which come from the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources. Five out of the seven members represent areas of fossil fuel production, not the nuclear industry. Yet this report is very supportive of nuclear energy in Canada because of its environmental benefits, economic advantages in parts of Canada, and its security and flexibility.

August 25, 1988
Oral Questions
Given today's increasing concerns of acid rain, dying maple trees, fishless lakes, and the greenhouse effect, nuclear energy must, and I emphasize must, have a role in meeting Canada's energy needs.

subsubtopic: PATRONAGE ALLEGATIONS-ALLEGED TELEPHONE CONVERSATION RECORDED BY MEMBER FOR ROSEMONT- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know they are talking about a strike at Canada Post, but 1 did not know the Government was on strike as well. At last, here comes the Deputy Prime Minister.
Mr. Speaker, during the last few days, we have tried to obtain clarification regarding the actions of the Prime Minister's chief of staff, especially in his conversations with the Hon. Member for Rosemont.
During that time, we have had four different versions from the Government.
In the first version the Prime Minister told us there was no threat. In the second version, the Deputy Prime Minister told us the purpose was to ask the Hon. Member for further details and to remind her of her duty to hand over any evidence she had to the police. Member is really reaching now. 1 know that he is trying to get his former colleague, Mr. Serge Joyal, elected to the House of Commons, so I suppose he is getting prompted from him. 1 have tried to answer all the pertinent questions relative to this matter as accurately as I possibly can. subtopic: RESIDENTS OF SAINT-BASILE-LE-GRAND AND AREA-REQUEST THAT SPECIAL HEALTH PROGRAM BE INSTITUTED
RESIDENTS OF SAINT-BASILE-LE-GRAND AND AREA-REQUEST THAT SPECIAL HEALTH PROGRAM BE INSTITUTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare but in his absence, I will direct it to the Deputy Prime Minister.
Yesterday, the explosion of 20,000 gallons of PCBs forced the evacuation of 3,500 people from their homes. We know that PCBs are highly toxic substances and that several experts are concerned about the likely consequences on the health of the people of Saint-Basile-le-Grand and the surrounding area.
Oral Questions
Can the Minister assure the residents of Saint-Basile-le-Grand and the vicinity that the federal Government will implement a special health research and follow-up program in order to determine both short and medium term, impact on all those affected by this accident?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subtopic: RESIDENTS OF SAINT-BASILE-LE-GRAND AND AREA-REQUEST THAT SPECIAL HEALTH PROGRAM BE INSTITUTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to assure the Hon. Member for Outremont and all Members of this House of the Government's extreme concern for the well-being of the citizens of Saint-Basile-le-Grand and the surrounding areas as a result of this tragic fire.
1 am sorry some Hon. Members opposite are not as concerned about this issue as the House should be. We are extremely concerned about the combustion of some 5,000 gallons of PCBs in a warehouse site in Saint-Basile-le-Grand. 1 can give the House a status report.
As we know, the fire has been extinguished and a cleanup is commencing. A fire investigation is under way as to the cause of this tragic event, and sampling and analytical work is ongoing. In fact, officials from the Department of the Environment were on site within half an hour of the first alarm and a full scientific team was on site first thing yesterday morning. They have been working with a committee of experts who were on the scene scientifically measuring the extent of contamination and any possible hazards that may result from this tragedy. The team includes a principal toxicologist, an expert in the matters of PCB contamination and its combustion, Dr. Albert Nantel, and Dr. Carriere, a local medical adviser who is familiar with these problems.
I can assure the House that the Government and the Minister of the Environment, who is at this very moment travelling to the site and will make a statement later today, are taking every necessary precaution to ensure the health of and the orderly reoccupation by the citizens when it is safe to do so.

Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to direct my suplementary question to the Deputy Prime Minister.

Will the Government reverse its decision and provide the
NRC with the funds it needs to accelerate research on ways

August 25, 1988
Oral Questions
and means to neutralize PCBs? It is a matter of urgent public interest.
Hon. Frank Oberle (Minister of State (Science and
Technology)): Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could answer this question. The Hon. Member made some erroneous utterings in her preamble.
There has not been the cut to the National Research Council she has alleged, nor has this particular program of PCB research been targeted for any cuts. In fact, research is going on, not just at the NRC but in government laboratories and universities, in ways to handle, dispose of, and store this dangerous substance. The Hon. Member's assertion is wrong. The Government is acting and research institutes are dealing with the problem.
