speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 cannot confirm the accuracy of the suggestion offered by the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party. As he knows, as part of the policy of eliminating PCBs from transformer systems across Canada, it is not legal to use and install such transformers. In fact, it could well be that there are some transformers still in operation, perhaps on the roofs of buildings, but this would not, I would imagine, be a storage situation.
Department of Environment officials have provided me with an assurance that the full inventory of PCB storage locations is available and regularly updated. As well, the Minister of the Environment, working with provincial Environment Ministers through the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers, has established specific storage sites outside urban areas, and there is, as the Hon. Member knows, a plan to remove all of these concentrations of stored PCBs to these safe sites. It is part of a federal-provincial initiative and an action plan which has been developed in consultation with provincial environment officials who have the legal and final authority within their provinces to ensure that these measures are fully complied with.

Mr. Speaker, I had confirmed for me just a while ago that there are indeed located on the roof of The Bay store in downtown Montreal some 20,000 litres of PCBs. This is a very dangerous substance and
it strikes one as dangerously serious in its implications if there should be a fire.
I am also told PCBs are stored in The Gazette building in downtown Montreal, perhaps on the roof again. I have also learned that until very recently, and we do not know when, there were 60,000 litres of PCBs stored by Air Canada at Dorval International Airport. I am told they were just moved recently and I would like the Minister to find out just how recently that was.
More concretely, with respect to the existing sites in the heart of Montreal, would the Minister confirm that the federal Department had a list of sites where these substances were stored? Will he also find out when the Government first learned of them being stored on the roof of The Bay store? In addition, could he tell us why the federal Government did not take action to have these PCBs removed from what was obviously an unsafe site in the centre of Montreal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the Hon. Leader of the NDP that the Government and the Minister will certainly be doing everything within their power and jurisdiction to see that such dangerous storage sites are eliminated from all urban areas of Canada. I am not able to confirm whether or not there are quantities of PCB coolant fluids on The Bay store in Montreal.
I do not think he would expect me to assure him of that today.
However, I can assure him that the Minister of the Environment, who is on his way to Montreal at this moment with the Minister of Transport, will be making a full statement after his arrival and inspection of the site, and should be able to clarify the extent to which there might be other similar storage sites in the Greater Montreal area. I certainly share the concern of all Members of this House over any such storage of PCBs in any of our cities.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT LIST OF STORAGE SITES BE MADE PUBLIC
REQUEST THAT LIST OF STORAGE SITES BE MADE PUBLIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am told that the Quebec Department of the Environment prepared a list of some 50 such sites in that province some time ago. There are known to be some 500 in the province of Ontario. I am also told that a former employee of the federal Department of the Environment, Mr. Marc Levy, lost his job not too long ago because of a conflict of interest in this respect, and he has since been involved in doing work for private gain in the storage of PCBs.
Given that, will the Minister assure us that the Minister of the Environment will make public tomorrow a complete list of the storage sites of this very dangerous substance so the people of Canada will know whether they are living in close proximity to such a site? Will he also assure us that the Government will take steps to make sure that all protective measures have been put in place, and that the Minister will make a comprehensive statement on federal government policy dealing with the present serious situation in Quebec, as well as outlining a policy for all of Canada?
August 25, 1988

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT LIST OF STORAGE SITES BE MADE PUBLIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot make undertakings on behalf of the Hon. Minister of the Environment in the House this afternoon. However, 1 can assure the Hon. Member that all of the available information, that is to say the inventory of PCB storage sites in Canada, is available to the Department of the Environment. Working with provincial environment officials through the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers, an action plan is being developed to do exactly what the Hon. Member has asked for.
At the same time I understand his concern and that of all Members, and in particular the residents of Saint-Basile-le-Grand, that something more urgent and immediate must be done. There is indeed an investigation under way into the circumstances of the fire and the necessary measures which must be taken to provide a measure of confidence to the displaced residents of this part of Montreal.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SASKATCHEWAN MINISTER OF ENERGY AND MINES

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SASKATCHEWAN MINISTER OF ENERGY AND MINES
speechtext: I wish to draw to the attention of Hon. Members the presence in our gallery of the Hon. Patricia Smith, Minister of Energy and Mines for the Province of Saskatchewan.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SASKATCHEWAN MINISTER OF ENERGY AND MINES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Yesterday the Minister of Employment categorically rejected the proposal to set up special adjustment programs for workers displaced by free trade. How can the Government support that position when the provinces, the Macdonald Commission, the C. D. Howe Institute, and others, along with two Standing Committees of this House, all recommended special adjustment programs? Is the Government going to let these workers fend for themselves after free trade?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: FREE TRADE-REQUEST FOR SPECIAL ADJUSTMENT PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows but refuses to accept, we have within the Canadian Jobs Strategy Program the flexibility to deal with labour adjustment in all of its categories. Five million workers a year are affected by changes in their jobs, in the workplace or in their work description now. There are going to be 251,000 new jobs created under free trade and it is our job to ensure that programs are in place to ensure workers can take advantage of those opportunities. I can assure the Hon. Member that no one
Oral Questions
has their interest at heart more than this Government and this Minister.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, is everyone else wrong and the Minister right? The present programs are not working. They are not adequate. Since 1984, the programs have been cut by 32 per cent, from $2.2 billion to $1.5 billion. They are not working and the proof lies in the fact that we have over 10 per cent unemployment in five of our provinces, yet we have a shortage of skilled workers in Ontario. If the programs are working why are we left with a situation like this? Why is the Government content to have that sort of program with the introduction of free trade?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member knows that regional differences in unemployment rates were not invented by this Government. Quite the reverse. Unemployment in all regions of Canada has come down since this Government came into office. If our training programs are so terribly bad, then why is unemployment at its lowest level in so many years?
The programs we have put in place are sufficient to deal not only with any adjustments that come with free trade, but also to prepare the Canadian people in the 1990s for a fast changing workforce. We are creating real jobs, not paint-the-fence jobs.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture and concerns the fire in Saint-Basile-le-Grand and its impact on the agricultural community.
It is our understanding that the Government of Quebec has quarantined animals from that area. Can he advise the House what action the federal Government is taking in its jurisdiction dealing with livestock in particular?

Mr. Speaker, I am not in a position at this moment to supply details other than to say that, immediately upon recognition of the incident, our people were on the scene and have been there since. They are working in full co-operation with the environmental and health and welfare people. From Canada's point of view, we have developed an action plan. When additional, detailed and accurate information is received from the environmental and health authorities, we will implement whatever action is necessary to ensure the health and safety of the Canadian consumer. We will also be involved if the area is designated a disaster area. If sufficient funds are provided to trigger the federal-provincial agreement, then Agriculture Canada will be fully involved on behalf of farmers and consumers.

August 25, 1988
Ora! Questions

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and is with regard to the compensation question. The Minister of Agriculture just indicated that the area could possibly be declared an emergency area under the normal rules of the Government of Canada and the Government of Quebec.
Will the Government indicate whether it is prepared to work with the Government of Quebec to provide compensation to those individuals who, through no fault of their own, have had personal effects, livestock, et cetera, destroyed, as well as a disruption of their lifestyle? Is the Government prepared to enter into an agreement with the Province of Quebec for compensation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 think the question is slightly premature. Not to in any way trivialize the nature of the event that has occurred, it is important, first, to have scientific teams on the site and to do a careful assessment of the extent of possible damage to the surrounding areas, the homes, the properties, the gardens, and the health of the individuals who must return to live in their community.
That assessment is under way. As I have indicated, there is a team of scientists taking and analyzing samples which are being reviewed on site by a committee of experts. Until we have a full report at the end of that process it would be premature to speculate on a particular level of compensation.
However, the Hon. Member and the House can be assured that the Government, as it always has, will meet its full measure of responsibility to live up to the genuine needs of people which arise from this tragic and unforeseen event.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Yesterday I spoke to the Minister regarding the plight of plant workers at Brig Bay, Newfoundland, and I thank the Minister for promising to investigate that situation.
Today I want to bring to the Minister's attention the crisis in the inshore fishery on the Northern and Burin Peninsulas of Newfoundland. In both these areas fishermen have not had enough earnings in the last 15 weeks to qualify for unemployment insurance this winter. They need either direct financial compensation, such as that given to farmers, or a job development program which will pay them a wage equivalent to what they would earn as fishermen during a normal fishing season.
Is the Minister prepared to direct her officials to investigate the situation in both the Burin and Great Northern Peninsulas of Newfoundland? Will she ask those officials to devise, on an emergency basis, an appropriate response to the needs of these fishermen in Newfoundland and Labrador?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question from the Hon. Member. We are watching the situation in Newfoundland and Labrador very carefully. As the Hon. Member knows, when there was a hardship of this nature in 1985 the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, were very involved in coming up with a solution, which solution was not an extension of UI benefits.
In answer to the question about investigating the situation, my officials will be meeting with his and he and I will be discussing the situation further.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY ASSESSMENT OF SITUATION

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY ASSESSMENT OF SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to point out to the Minister that there is very little resemblance between this situation and that in 1985. In 1985 we were talking about workers who had had a season which ended short of the 10 weeks required to qualify for unemployment insurance. This year we are talking about workers who have had only one or two weeks of earnings in the last 15.
It is not only a matter of having income this winter, it is a matter of having the funds to put bread and butter on the table now. It is a real crisis, in particular on the Burin and Great Northern Peninsulas of Newfoundland.
I ask the Minister not to wait until November 15 to do an assessment but to direct her officials to do an emergency assessment now and to find a way to assist fishermen and their families now, many of whom have children going back to school in a few weeks, to put bread and butter on the table and to do all the things that any Canadian has to do to prepare
August 25, 1988

their families for school in the fall and to get through the coming winter months.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY ASSESSMENT OF SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my colleague, the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration, has said, her officials and mine are examining the circumstances which could lead to the necessity of such an emergency program. I am pleased to have been a part of the decision making which led to the program in 1986 which my colleague mentioned. I believe there was a smaller program in 1987 in other parts of Newfoundland.
However, it has never been our policy to announce assistance, which could well be more greatly needed later in the year, when the fishing season is still under way.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY ASSESSMENT OF SITUATION
speechtext: They are hungry now.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY ASSESSMENT OF SITUATION
speechtext: There are still fishermen from the Labrador Straits and the Great Northern Peninsula fishing off the coast of Labrador. As the Hon. Member for St. John's West pointed out in this House last week, the Newfoundland fishery has produced much higher financial benefits and landings in total than it did last year. We will certainly give very serious consideration to the needs in the areas to which he has referred, the Burin Peninsula and the Labrador Straits region of Newfoundland.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance about the increase in interest rates. Despite the pleas of Canada's Premiers last week, the Bank of Canada has today raised the bank rate again and three of Canada's chartered banks have raised their prime rate by one-half of a per cent to 11.25 per cent.
Does the Government intend to take any action to roll back these increases in bank interest rates, or has the Government told its friends in the banks that they can jack up their interest rates because there will not be an election this fall?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is putting a wrong motivation in his question. I think Canadians would accept the fact that we have provided good economic management. That is very evident in the economic policy and results over the last four years.
Hear, hear!

We do have the challenge now of increasing inflationary pressures. We have options. We could ignore the problem as the Liberals did in the seventies. We know that that led us to the very high levels of inflation and the consequent high interest rates in 1981-82. Or, we could take a far-sighted, responsible, prudent approach and head off the problem now before it becomes the serious crisis
Oral Questions
that it was in 1981-82. That is the prudent policy to follow and that is what good economic management is all about.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance seems unaware that, last week, Statistics Canada reported that inflation had gone down in almost every region in Canada. Despite this, the Government supports increases in the interest rates charged by the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks. Why is the government not willing to do something to stop this increase in the interest rates charged by the chartered banks? Does the Government consider the advice given by the premiers of no value? Why does the Government push for higher interest rates despite their harmful effects on home-building and home-buying, on farmers already suffering from drought in the West and on investment and especially job creation in poorer regions?
Mr. Speaker, I think Canadians understand that there is a clear link between inflation and high interest rates.
Yeah, the higher the rate, the higher the inflation.

I ask Hon. Members to think back to 1981-82. I have some newspaper headlines which might be helpful to Hon. Members "Chances receding in fight with inflation", "Acceptance of inflation seems to be getting the upper hand", "Can we beat inflation?", "Inflation now a fact of life". That was after the Liberal Government of the day allowed inflationary pressures to get out of hand.
There is another headline to which I want to refer the Hon. Member, that is, "Realism, responsibility needed to cure inflation". That is the approach we are following as a Government and that will be evident in the economic results in the years ahead.

subsubtopic: LOCATION OF PROPOSED PRISON IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question concerns the Government's announcement yesterday that Newfoundland's new federal prison will be built in Harbour Grace, a Tory riding, rather than in Buchans. Would the Solicitor General explain what criteria were used in the decision to switch the location of the prison from Buchans to Harbour Grace? Can he explain to the people of Buchans and the people of Canada whether the same criteria were used in this particular decision as were used in the decision to locate the prison in Port Cartier, in the Prime Minister's riding?

August 25, 1988
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. James Kelleher (Solicitor General of Canada):
subsubtopic: LOCATION OF PROPOSED PRISON IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is making an assumption that we switched the prison site from Buchans. We never selected Buchans as the site.
The Commissioner of Corrections set up a site selection committee and, using that criteria, they investigated a number of sites across Newfoundland, including Buchans. After reviewing the work of the site selection committee, the Commissioner recommended to me that the Harbour Grace area be selected, and I accepted that recommendation.

Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General knows that money had already been designated in the 1984-85 Estimates for a federal penitentiary in Buchans. He also knows that this new location was chosen even before land was acquired, even before the federal Government was in a position to build a prison there.
The Minister for International Trade said today: "The federal Government cannot justify putting a prison in a community like Buchans which is nowhere near where prisoners' families are living". If this is the policy of the Government of Canada, how can the Solicitor General justify the building of the Prime Minister's prison in a remote part of his riding, in Port Cartier, 900 kilometres away from Montreal, a 14-hour bus ride away from Quebec City? If the consideration is close proximity to family, why was the Prime Minister's prison built where it is?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Kelleher (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am extremely surprised that the Member complains about us not selecting Buchans as the site for the prison when the former Solicitor General also rejected that site and selected an area in Windsor.
I have here a press release dated August 7, 1984, in which the former Solicitor General, the Member for York Centre, announced that a penitentiary would be built in Newfoundland. "We are going to initiate an assessment of possible sites in the Windsor area later this week and it is expected that a suitable piece of property will be acquired within the next couple of months".
They did what we have done. They rejected the Buchans site because it did not contain a suitable infrastructure. I find it a little difficult that the Member complains now when what we did was what the former Solicitor General of his Government did.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General who will know that
in 1984, the Liberal Party decided to build a federal penitentiary in a Liberal riding.
Retract that.
Now we see a Tory Government building a federal penitentiary in a Tory riding. I want to ask the Minister-
What about Jack Harris?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Burnaby.

In view of the fact that the Prime Minister decided to build a prison in his own constituency, supposedly for economic benefit, if that is the same criteria for the Minister how can he explain on economic grounds not building the federal penitentiary either in the Buchans area or Bell Island area, both of which have desperately high levels of unemployment? Why one standard for the Prime Minister and another standard for the people of Newfoundland?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Kelleher (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I explained earlier in the House, the site of Harbour Grace was recommended to me by the Commissioner of Corrections after his site selection committee had reviewed various possible sites in Newfoundland. One of the sites they looked at was indeed the Buchans area. However, they determined that the required infrastructure was not present in Buchans but was indeed present in the St. John's region or Harbour Grace area. That is the reason for it.
Certainly Buchans was considered, and indeed the Commissioner of Corrections met personally with the mayor and other members from that community, and listened to them carefully and considered their site.

Mr. Speaker, if this is suddenly a concern, why was the Government prepared to spend $42 million extra to build a federal prison in the Prime Minister's constituency? What exactly are the standards for prison construction by the Government? Is it economic benefit, correctional criteria, or is it in fact trying desperately to save the ridings of Tory Members of Parliament? Is that not the real reason?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Kelleher (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned earlier, the site selection committee determined that Buchans did not contain the necessary infrastructure, which includes access to court facilities, medical and psychological hospitals, doctors and emergency services such as police, fire, and national defence. The Buchans area does not contain that infrastructure. The Harbour Grace area does.
In addition, CSC recommends that a community must have
a minimum population of at least 2,500. Buchans barely has
1,000, and the Harbour Grace area which has been selected
August 25, 1988

has a population of approximately 12,000 to 13,000. It is indeed a most acceptable site.

Mir. Alan Redway (York East): Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. According to senior officials with Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Metropolitan Toronto area housing crisis is a result of the fact that land for housing is not coming on the market fast enough. They say that one of the major reasons for that is that six companies own all of the development land in the Metro Toronto area.
Will the Minister advise the House if CMHC has asked his officials to investigate whether there has been a breach of the Competition Act? If they have not done so, will the Minister give us his undertaking that he will do so?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: HOUSING SITUATION IN TORONTO-OWNERSHIP OF DEVELOPMENT LAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am not entirely sure whether CMHC has asked officials in my Department in that regard. However, the Director of Investigation of the Competition Bureau is aware of the situation and is investigating it.
Due to the confidentiality provisions of the Competition Act, I really cannot say any more in that regard, except that it is being investigated by the Director of Investigation of the Competition Bureau.

subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF UKRAINIAN REFUGEE STATUS CLAIMANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. The Minister will know that several weeks ago a group of 205 Ukrainians en route to Rome from Poland claimed refugee status in Vienna and are currently being held in an Austrian refugee camp, faced with possible deportation back to Poland.
The Minister will also know that the group wants to come to Canada and that the Ukrainian Canadian community has made extensive representations to the Minister for Government sponsorship of these refugees. In view of the fact that in recent years there have been virtually no Government sponsored Ukrainian refugees from eastern Europe, will the Minister advise the House whether the Government of Canada is prepared to accept and sponsor these refugees to Canada? Will she seek immediate assurances from the Austrian
Oral Questions
Government that the group will not be deported to any country behind the Iron Curtain?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF UKRAINIAN REFUGEE STATUS CLAIMANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member and other Members for their interest in this case. As the Hon. Member knows, people of Ukrainian background coming from eastern Europe have either Polish papers or papers from the Soviet Union. These particular cases were brought to our attention. We spent considerable time in an effort to assist them.
The applications are currently being processed, including medical and security procedures. Those procedures will apply. The process is under way. We have already been in contact with the Austrian Government and we are assured that no one will be deported to Poland.
We have asked for assistance from the Ukrainian community, with whom I am meeting next week on this issue, in identifying any cases of special hardship. I understand there are none, but if some are brought to our attention we will certainly process those on a priority basis. Our expectation is that these people, providing the process goes smoothly and all the people are cleared, will be arriving in Canada this winter or this spring.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of the Environment my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Last week we brought to the attention of the Government the publication of a U.S. Congressional study with respect to the impact on human health of lead in gasoline. Today we learned about a study undertaken by Dr. Anthony McMichael at the University of Adelaide in Australia to the effect that there is new evidence that exposure to relatively low levels of lead during early childhood can slow and perhaps permanently stifle mental development. Therefore, the question 1 must again ask of the Government is whether it is prepared at last to advance the target date for reducing lead in gasoline from January 1993 to 1990.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can certainly assure the Hon. Member that the National Health and Welfare experts, as well as Environment Canada officials, are studying the brief prepared by the Canadian Coalition for Lead Free Gasoline with respect to the effect of high lead levels on the health of children. There will be consideration given to a accelerated phase-out if that proves to be necessary.

August 25, 1988
Oral Questions
1 should point out that the program, with the deadline of 1992, to eliminate lead in gasoline, was a program introduced by the Government of which the Hon. Member was a member at the time. Since that time, the safe blood lead level of concern has been lowered from 20 micrograms per decalitre in 1986, to 10 to 15 micrograms now. But we have seen a lowering of the actual levels in children in urban cities to a level of 8 micrograms per decalitre from 12 micrograms which was the level in 1984.
In other words, we are making regular progress and the research to which the Hon. Member referred has certainly been reviewed by officials in the Department of National Health and Welfare and in the Department of the Environment to see if further measures are necessary.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister has pulled out the wrong briefing note. 1 am referring to more recent studies. In view of the fact that the Royal Society of Canada cautioned the Government that the program that is now in place may not be fast enough, is the Government willing to make a decision and advance the deadline for further reduction of lead in gasoline from 1993 to 1990? That is the question the Minister ought to answer.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member may feel I am reading from the wrong briefing note, but my answer to the first question he asked was nonetheless correct. The Government is looking at recent scientific evidence and the report of the Coalition on Lead in Gasoline with a view to determining whether a faster phase-out is necessary. 1 think the Hon. Member would have to agree that it would be irresponsible for a Minister to stand up in the House and promise to change the deadline date of a program his Government established without doing our homework first.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay- Nipigon with a single question, followed by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North with a single question.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport. Mr. Ian Gillies of the Cargill Grain Company said recently that although it is actually cheaper by over $8 per tonne to ship grain from southern Manitoba to the St. Lawrence terminal elevators than to the West Coast terminals, the federal subsidy paid to railways makes the cost to the shipper over $12 less to rail this Manitoba grain to the West Coast.
Can the Parliamentary Secretary confirm the accuracy of Mr. Gillies' statement which suggests that the railways' subsidies paid under the Western Grain Transportation Act
have a dramatically distorting effect on economic activity in the Canadian grain trade?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry St. Germain (Minister of State (Transport)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first, 1 would like to correct the situation. I am not the Parliamentary Secretary. I am the Minister of State for Transport.
Oh, oh!
Not for long.
Some things are better left unsaid.

I thank the Hon. Member for having given prior advice of the question. With respect to the Hon. Member's question, as the Hon. Member knows I have met delegations from his riding with respect to the port authorities and the shipping people who work out of and represent that area. We are concerned. Member, and we look forward to the response and recommendations with respect to this matter.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the President of the Treasury Board I would like to direct my question to the Deputy Prime Minister. The vast majority of the public servants who are represented by the Public Service Alliance and the Professional Institute know their collective agreements with the Government ran out in 1987. They have been negotiating with officials of the Treasury Board since then. They have not had a single offer in respect to the salary part of their agreement. They have asked repeatedly to meet with the President of the Treasury Board and have been told that she is either too sick or too tired to meet with them.
Would the Deputy Prime Minister make it his business to see that a cabinet Minister who has some authority meets with the representatives of these two organizations so that the bargaining can be brought to a successful conclusion? The fact is that the morale of our employees is going to go down and down unless there is some movement.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of State and Minister of State (Treasury Board)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to advise that the bargaining process is continuing. We all regret that we have not been able to reach a conclusion to the bargaining process, but there has never been a suggestion that the bargaining on either side is continuing in bad faith. I think we should leave it with the officials and with the representatives of the unions, with the hope that very soon they will be able to negotiate a final position and execute an agreement.
August 25, 1988
Point of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before we get to the point of order, I should like to say Hon. Members have been very co-operative. The Hon. Member for Algoma has a single question and that is the end of Question Period. 1 then must hear the Hon. Minister on a point of order. The Hon. Member for York Centre also has a point of order. And we will get it all done.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF DROUGHT IN SOUTHWESTERN ONTARIO-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister in the absence of the Minister of Agriculture. It concerns the drought situation which has afflicted southwestern Ontario and other parts of the province. Last month the Minister of Agriculture said that assistance would be provided to eastern farmers on the same basis as those in western Canada where some $153 million was provided to the livestock industry alone. The estimates of losses in Ontario now approach $.75 billion, that is $750 million of losses in crops. I wonder if the Deputy Prime Minister could indicate what assistance is going to be provided and when that assistance is going to be provided?
The Minister of Agriculture failed to show up for a very important meeting a week ago with farm representatives. All the important farm representatives of various organizations are meeting in Guelph today. He said: The purpose of this motion is to make our tax legislation more consistent and to apply the same approach taken in other areas to the area of child care expenses. Mr. Speaker, as you know, all personal exemptions such as deductions for dependants and children have been turned into tax credits, which seemed only fair. In fact, I recommended as much, if I am not mistaken, in my first speech in the House, in response to the first Budget Speech when we were talking about tax reform. I said that it would be fairer and more equitable to turn these exemptions into tax credits, thus setting a fairer value on these exemptions and making them a better reflection of the expenses to be covered. Since tax rates differ depending on one's income bracket, the exemption tended to be more generous to people on high incomes than to those on lower incomes. The Government agreed with this proposal, except that when it got to the matter of child care expenses, instead of transforming deductions for child care expenses into tax credits, the Government maintained the deduction formula.
If adopted, Motion No. 3 would, first of all, transform the deduction into a tax credit. We know that currently, the deduction is $2,000. This Bill will raise the deduction to $4,000 for children up to the age of 6, but only for families who provide receipts. If you hire someone and you have receipts for child care expenses, you can deduct up to $4,000 annually for children up to the age of 6. Before, there was a maximum of $8,000 per family. That will disappear. We know that a family that incurs child care expenses but does not have receipts, or where one of the spouses stays home to look after the children, can obtain a maximum increase of $200 annually of the refundable child tax credit. However, this applies only to families on lower incomes.
I have no problem with this second part of the Act; since it is in keeping with what already existed and the tax credit continues and is refundable, no problem. But regarding the expense deduction, we believe that it would be preferable to have some consistency and keep the tax credit approach as much as possible. And since it is a tax credit that helps families, we believe that this tax credit applicable to child care expenses should be 26 per cent. For example, a family with $2,000 in child care expenses would be entitled to a tax credit of 26 per cent of $2,000; if it has $4,000 in child care expenses, it would be entitled to a tax credit of 26 per cent. That is my proposal. It does not change the ceiling, but simply changes the deduction into a proportional tax credit. Why 26 per cent? Because it would help families with modest incomes more. Under the present tax reform, their income is taxed at 17 per cent. The first $27,500 of refundable income and a 26 per cent tax credit would thus benefit families making $27,500 or less and would change nothing, or very little, for families with more substantial incomes.
August 25, 1988

So I make this proposal for two purposes: first, to keep some consistency in the use of tax credits, since the Government has decided to eliminate exemptions and to change them into tax credits, 1 do not see why this should not be done for child care expenses; second, it would enable families with child care expenses who are in the lowest income bracket to obtain a 26 per cent tax credit for them.

Mr. Speaker, 1 was just given a very sober nod from the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin). I hope he realizes that it is you, Mr. Speaker, and not he who consents to my being able to speak in the House of Commons.
This motion from the Liberal Party is like the curate's egg. It has some good portions and some that are not so good. The aim is to make the child care deduction into a refundable tax credit at the rate of 26 per cent of eligible child care expenses. This particular clause of the Bill, Clause 39 which amends Section 63 of the Income Tax Act, previously provided for the deduction of child care expenses to the limit of $2,000 per child under seven years of age. This has been raised in the Government's proposals to a maximum of $4,000 per child under seven years of age or a maximum of two-thirds of the taxpayer's earned income. The Liberal amendment proposes that that be turned into a refundable tax credit at the rate of 26 per cent of eligible child care expenses.
The NDP is of the view that we need to make sure child care spaces are available across the country. To act almost exclusively through the tax system as proposed by the Government is not good enough. By increasing the allowable amount from $2,000 to $4,000 we are providing a benefit to wealthy Conservatives who pay nannies to look after their children and then deduct the entire amount. Or, perhaps they are wealthy enough that they can pay for day care at full rates. However, there are an awful lot of people who do not have that kind of money.
In addition, like it or not, there is an informal child care network which has grown up because of the lack of more formal facilities. In that network it is not always possible to get receipts. If you do not get receipts, you do not get a credit. In addition to which, the wealthier you are, the more this $4,000 per child deduction is going to be worth. A secretary earning $20,000 a year who pays $4,000 or $5,000 for child care will be able to get a credit only at the rate of 17 per cent of that amount. It is worth about $680 to her, or about $15 a week. If the over-all tax system was fair, if there had not been concessions to people who are wealthy, if there had not been this very large tax-free zone on capital gains, again to people who are wealthy, it might be acceptable for the Government to tell senior citizens that everyone has to make a few sacrifices and that the investment income deduction has to go because that is part of the give and take, part of the trade-offs which occur with tax reform.

They see that the Government has reduced taxes by $4,300 annually for taxpayers with an annual income in excess of $100,000, while people on modest incomes, like senior citizens and people with an annual income of $15,000 to $20,000, get a tax reduction of about $2,000 and maybe not more than that.

Mr. Speaker, this is why senior citizens' organizations brought their requests and proposals before the Committee on Finance which examined this Bill, urging the Government to maintain the $1,000 investment income deduction. Members of our Party have consistently proposed that the tax system be examined and revised and made much more fair than it is. The Carter Commission, appointed by former Prime Minister Diefenbaker, made it clear that the tax system had been changed so many times and so many special exemptions had been given to corporations and wealthy individuals, that it was completely broken down in terms of being fair. When this Government started to talk about implementing a fairer tax system, a reform of the tax system, as it was called, we watched with a great deal of interest to see what would happen.

I want to give one illustration of what has happened to one very wealthy individual in this country as a result of the tax policies of the former Liberal Government and the present Conservative Government. I refer to Mr. Robert Campeau. He was quoted in a news story which appeared in The Globe and Mail on May 12, 1988. It reads:
"He told the Canadian Club of Montreal that Canada's deficit is 7 to 8 per cent of gross national product, compared with only 2.5 per cent in the United States. And he said Canada's Government-supported medicare is a mistake.
"I question whether politicians, federal or provincial, who put in medicare were really thinking of the welfare of the people, or were they, perhaps, thinking of their own political welfare."
The article concludes:
He lashed out at the regulatory burden business faces in Canada and demanded that social welfare programs be examined and rationalized.
Let us look at Mr. Robert Campeau. In the 1960s, he was a developer and builder of houses. He owned 4,000 acres of land around Ottawa and had built 11,000 homes. In the years since then, he was able, by contracts given to him by Liberal governments, often without the Government calling for bids, to build and then rent to governments some of the largest office buildings in the National Capital Region. According to information obtained by then Conservative Members of Parliament, including the late Walter Baker, Ron Huntington from Vancouver and the present Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay), when they were in opposition, the rents agreed to were substantially higher than the going rates in the area.
The Guy Favreau complex in Montreal, the largest government building in Montreal and perhaps the largest in Canada, was built by Mr. Campeau through a lease and buy-back arrangement with the then Liberal Government. The present Auditor General described it as one of the most wasteful federal projects he had ever seen. According to the Montreal Gazette yesterday, the rent on the building is just under $1 million a month, and bricks from the walls are falling. According to a senior official in the Department of Public Works, all the bricks on the building may have to be replaced.
Using the profits Mr. Campeau was permitted and encouraged to make in Canada, he entered the United States and has become one of the most active and successful developers in the United States. He is now operating in the multibillion dollar class. How was he able to do it? Partly because of the favourable contracts he received from Liberal governments, but also because of the kind of tax system we have.
We did a search and found that from 1978, which was the earliest information we were able to find, to 1985, net profits for Campeau Corporation totalled more than $125 million. Yet, according to The Financial Post data, in 1978, the company paid no corporation taxes at all. In fact, it received a tax credit. Since then it has not paid one penny in current taxes.

Every one of the years from 1978, on have been profitable years for the company. From 1985, alone, the company recorded net profits of $27.9 million, yet no taxes were paid. Unfortunately, this Government has refused to accept the notion of a dollar is a dollar is a dollar when it comes to tax policies. So that a dollar earned through a capital gains increase is treated quite differently from a dollar that is earned by a wage earner or a dollar that is earned in terms of dividend payments.
We are saying that as long as these inequities exist in the tax field, we are darn well going to fight to help those, particularly senior citizens, who stand to lose their $1,000 exemption from interest earned.
The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) has attempted to put on the record the great benefits that senior citizens have received because of tax reform. Of course, he is

very selective in terms of comparing taxes paid in one year as compared to the next year. Of course, what the Government insists on doing, in attempting to show that seniors and other taxpayers are saving money because of tax reform, is to compare the taxes that they paid in 1987 to what they will pay in 1988 with tax reform. Lo and behold, yes, many of them will be paying less.
If you can compare it to 1984, when this Government was elected, those taxpayers are all paying more, and that is the truth of the matter.
The taxes that they are paying, both on income tax and on sales tax, have increased because of this Government. The Government as well fails to mention that even when the taxes paid from 1977 to 1988, are compared, the taxes that the average Canadian tax earner is paying on the goods and services that he is buying are, of course, not included. One of the things that this Government did when it introduced tax reform and lowered the rates on income taxes paid, was to have also increased the sales taxes to make up for the loss in revenue.
So, yes, you have seen a decrease in the income tax that you have paid, but you have also seen an increase in the taxes that you pay every time that you buy a chocolate bar, some clothes, a gallon of gasoline or whatever it may be. This Government is now taxing you in a way that Canadians have never been taxed before. That of course is the first year. If this Government is ever re-elected, the second shoe will drop. That will be a universal sales tax, in which everybody going for a haircut or a shoe shine or going to the dentist will also be taxed on whatever goods or services they will be purchasing.
When this Government talks about the benefit of tax reform to the seniors, it takes a very narrow view in trying to establish its case that seniors are better off. If you take an honest view, if you compare what the seniors and the average Canadian taxpayer is paying, both in income tax and in sales tax in 1984, when this Government was first elected, and what they are paying now under the so-called tax reform, in 1988, you will find that the average Canadian taxpayer of course pays substantially more.

progressivity and fairness in the tax system, yes, it is bad. Mr. Speaker. 1 appreciate the opportunity to join briefly in the debate on Motion Nos. 5 and 6 that were put forward by my colleague from Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy).
I want to focus particularly on his proposal that the $1,000 interest and investment income exemption in the income tax be continued. I want to do that on behalf of many of my constituents who have called me and have written to me about the kind of taxation that they have faced in the last year or two.
I remember how in the spring of 1987 many of the seniors looked at their income returns and considered the limited incomes that many of them have, perhaps with a pension plan and some investment income that they had received and had been able to build up over the years-not a great deal of money in many cases-enabling them to have a reasonably decent retirement. It allowed them to lead the kind of life that all of us are proud of having been able to achieve for senior citizens over the last 10 or 15 years, a good part, of course, because of the indexation of the old age pension which this Government tried, within a year of its election, to limit, not to do away with it completely.
These senior citizens found themselves over a year ago being hit with taxes. The taxes were not necessarily a great amount but the seniors were shocked that, their incomes not being very large and needing every cent to maintain themselves, they were having to pay tax. 1 have been sent by one or two constituents quite detailed statements of the kinds of incomes they had had for several years past. Their incomes had not improved markedly, probably had not kept up with inflation. But these senior citizens had paid very little, if any, tax until a year or
two into the life of the present Government and then there they were having to pay tax.
This is the experience of individuals and couples in Thunder Bay like those in every city and town and community across the country, that under this Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) the Government has been wringing out of individuals, middle and lower income Canadians, every cent of income tax possible. The Government has done that without being prepared to recognize that the pressure for revenue ought to make for tax fairness, for applying to corporations something halfway like the kind of brutal search for revenue that has been applied to lower income Canadians and the poor of this country who should not have to pay tax at all.
That is the context and the background against which we consider whether the $1,000 investment and interest income exemption should be continued or removed. The Minister of Finance knows that the Government of Canada needs revenue for all kinds of purposes. He has been cutting back in many areas and not living up to the challenges that face the Government. He has been niggardly with financing of post-secondary education and health care. The Minister, who knows how much he needs income, should have remembered about the $500,000 capital gains tax holiday he gave some Canadians in his attempt to make more millionaires, as he suggested a couple of years ago. If he had been fair and treated every dollar like every other dollar, putting the burden fairly everywhere to raise the revenue he wanted, senior citizens and persons who have built up some investment and drawn income therefrom should not have been touched. But when the boots have been put to lower and middle-income Canadians the way they have by this Government as I have described, it is unconscionable and absolutely unfair to take away the $1,000 interest income exemption as the Minister of Finance proposes to do.
It is those human reasons that involve the lives of seniors in my city, persons who have built up a certain amount through their own savings over the years, who deserve to enjoy the income from small investments. If the Minister of Finance is not going to be fair about it, let us continue that exemption and allow seniors to enjoy the fruits of their savings and of denying themselves in the past in order to build up these investments.
I feel very strongly the political necessity of the motion put forward by my friend, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it gives me the greatest of pleasure to move third reading of Bill C-205, an Act to protect heritage railway stations. Amended in a legislative committee, this Bill
Heritage Railway Stations
was presented to the House on July 15 by the chairperson of that committee, the Hon. Member for Leeds-Grenville (Mrs. Cossitt).
The significance of railways in shaping our nation's destiny cannot be denied. Railways brought Canada into existence and, in large part, they have defined our fundamental character. Because of Canada's size, geographical diversity, dependence on trade and the twin needs of settlement and political identity, transportation has been of vital importance to us. It is above all railway transportation which has been the very backbone of our nation. It is the railway station that remains the most cherished of the tangible reminders of what Canada's railways have meant to Canada and her people.
These stations were points of departure and arrival for thousands of families as they travelled on odysseys of settlement across our enormous country. They saw the farewells of tens of thousands of Canadian troops who went off to fight in four wars, and they were the first thing that those who returned saw when they came back home. Railway stations have been the scenes of millions of journeys undertaken by Canadians from all walks of life, and they figure in the memories of millions of Canadians. So the distress of Canadians when these stations are destroyed is completely understandable. We will be a poorer nation if our railway stations are lost.
Railways were our "national dream", and the heritage of our railways is the heritage of that dream. It has often been said that a nation will be judged by what it consciously chooses to preserve. Therefore, should not Canada strive to save examples of the very buildings that speak so eloquently to the role of the railway in the birth and the growth of this country, our heritage railway stations?
The answer is undeniably yes. But we must move quickly. Our stock of heritage railway stations is rapidly diminishing, and if nothing is done soon there may be nothing left to preserve. That is the purpose of the Bill currently before us, to provide a mechanism whereby the preservation of Canada's heritage railway stations may be assured.
This Bill would forbid a railway company from destroying or in any way altering a heritage railway station or its heritage features unless authorized by the Governor in Council. Failure to seek authorization would result in a fine.
What is a heritage railway station? This Bill defines a heritage railway station as a railway station designated as such; that is to say, a railway station that has been designated a heritage railway station on the recommendation of the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada.

August 25, 1988
Heritage Railway Stations
Here may 1 say that the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada is most interested in this Bill. The board has often expressed concern that our railway stations are disappearing. While this Bill, when passed, will add new responsibilities to those which it has had traditionally, the board has indicated that it is pleased to have a role to play in the identification and preservation of Canada's heritage railway stations. The board will move quickly to establish criteria to identify potential heritage railway stations so that it may deal with applications for designation in an effective and timely manner.
Now, if 1 may, I would like to say a special word of thanks to those who have made special contributions to Bill C-205, the Bill before us today. First, the former Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park, Mr. Flis, first introduced the Bill in 1984. There are the Members of this House who, during the course of debate on this Bill, spoke so movingly of the need to preserve heritage railway stations, those stations that are so close to the hearts of so many Canadians.
Beyond that, I would like to thank the chairperson of the legislative committee, the Hon. Member for Leeds-Grenville (Mrs. Cossitt) and the members of her committee, for the thoughtful and expeditious manner in which they dealt with this extremely important matter. I believe that the amendments resulting from committee consideration of Bill C-205 have strengthened the Bill in that they have addressed a number of technical difficulties, provided for clarification and will ensure ease of implementation of the Bill.
1 also want to say a special thank you to the Parliamentary Secretary for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Thacker) and to the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). The Hon. Member for Regina West worked so hard for this Bill that sometimes I wondered if it was not his Bill, he was so enthusiastic about it. I thank him for that enthusiasm and that hard work. I would also like to thank the Heritage Canada Foundation, the very life of which depends on heritage. The Foundation has done a tremendous job in supporting this Bill.
I would like to thank CP Rail, CN and VIA for appearing as witnesses, as did the Heritage Canada Foundation, before the committee and the Ministers of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) and of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) for giving so freely of the time of their departmental officials at committee stage.
The time for rhetoric is over. We must now take that final step and pass Bill C-205, an Act to protect heritage railway stations. If we fail to do so, a vitally important aspect of our national heritage and indeed of our national consciousness, our heritage railway stations, will remain prey to the vagaries of corporate decision-makers and will have at best an insecure future, or at worst, no future at all. If we fail to act and these buildings, be they humble structures in tiny hamlets or grand architectural monuments in urban centres, are lost, we will
have robbed future generations of what is rightfully their legacy.
Heritage railway stations must be preserved unimpaired for future generations, and 1 would urge the Members of this House unanimously to express their support for the Bill before us and to pass it from this House without further ado. Moreover, I would like to ask the Members of the Senate, for their part, to deal with Bill C-205 in an expeditious manner in order that the preservation of this nation's heritage railway stations may be assured.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I want to thank all Hon. Members for their support. I now move third reading of Bill C-205, an Act to protect heritage railway stations.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, 1 take much pleasure in rising in support of Bill C-205 which was sponsored by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). It is a good Bill and it is long overdue.
There were many previous occasions in previous years when Hon. Members of this place from all Parties tried various and sundry ways and means of preserving railway stations as heritage sites to be refurbished or used to handle passengers. I want to compliment the Hon. Member for Bow River and say that the Bill has the full support of my caucus and my Party.
I must mention at this point a long-held dream of mine. I solicit the support of my colleague from Bow River and any other of his colleagues to finally get the beautiful old Union Station in downtown Regina converted into a multi-modal transportation centre. I have been working on this since about 1970, and there are so many players in the piece that it took years to get them all together. First the CPR was involved, then VIA Rail came into the piece and then the CTC, the Department of Transport, the City of Regina, the Saskatchewan Transportation Company, the provincial Government, and two or three others I have probably overlooked.
At one point, it looked as though we had finally gotten it together. The federal Government was prepared to put up $500,000 toward the cost of refurbishing that old station. We were to build an addition on one end for a bus administration office of about six stories and one wing of the station would be the bus terminal. The central part would be where rail passengers embarked and disembarked. There would be two or three travel agencies, a nice little restaurant and perhaps some boutiques and shops.
I am just as angry at the former NDP Government of Saskatchewan as I am at the present Conservative Government of Saskatchewan. The NDP Government dragged its feet, hummed and hawed and horsed around, but finally in February, 1982, an agreement was signed. In June, 1982, there was a change of government and the Government changed its mind. The agreement went out of the window. Now we are going to have to do the whole darn thing all over again.

In supporting this Bill, I put in my plea for help from Members from all sides of the House. 1 sure have not given up on it. It is one of several reasons why I am running again.
I also want to pay tribute to the Hon. Member for Bow River. You know, Sir, how all of us get labeled around here. I am labelled a rabid, wild-eyed, left wing socialist-communist in disguise, according to the labels.
More!

The Hon. Member for Bow River gets labeled just like other Members as a wild-eyed, right wing fascist, et cetera. Yes, there are left wing and right wing fascists.
In any case, the hon. gentleman and I have sat on the Standing Committee on Transport all the years he has been here. He has not been here quite as long as 1 have, but he has been around a heck of a lot longer than anyone else in this place or any other place. We sat in committee many a time and kicked the heck out of each other. A few times we agreed. This is a good example of that. We worked together, confounded the bureaucrats and the governments and the fancy lawyers from the railroads and a few others. In spite of all that, or perhaps because of it, the Hon. Member has with this legislation left a good legacy behind him. I say that because I understand he is not running again.
I wish I was in as good a physical shape as he is. He can run around the block and I can barely walk it. However, I believe since 1935 or 1939, I am not sure which, he sat as a Member of the Alberta Legislature, was Minister of Highways for some 17 years, and I noticed that he did not try to get away with some of the nonsense we hear nowadays from some Tories about privatization and turning highway construction over to the private sector and whatnot. He built a lot of good highways with good people in his own department. He had then and has now a reputation for honesty and integrity in his service to the public of Alberta and Canada.
Hear, hear!

That is something all of us need to emulate, whether or not we agree with the Hon. Member, and it was not too often that we did. However, he has earned the respect and regard of people in this place, the Alberta Legislature, and certainly all of western Canada. The legacy the Hon. Member is leaving behind will serve in his stead everywhere in Canada.
When I think of the thousands of locations where the two railways destroyed beautiful old buildings, I realize it is a historical and social tragedy. This legislation stops them cold. They cannot touch these buildings without someone's okay. I think it is to the everlasting credit of the Hon. Member that he took this initiative. It was a pleasure for me and my friend from the Liberal Party to support him on the issue. We took part in committee hearings, questioned witnesses, and only accepted amendments that the Hon. Member for Bow River was prepared to accept. We got it through, and I commend the Bill to the House.
Heritage Railway Stations
I also commend the Hon. Member for Bow River. I hope no other Conservatives in the House learn how to survive as long as he has. I also hope he will not teach them. However, I do mean quite sincerely what I say about him and about this legislation, and I hope it can go through now.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to take a few moments of the House's time to add my congratulations to our valuable and senior colleague from Bow River (Mr. Taylor) on his initiative which will ensure that our railroad heritage is in part maintained.
I do this for two or three reasons. First, I and my family have a long-standing interest in heritage matters. We live in a designated heritage home. I have had the privilege of being on the Rideau Heritage Board. I was a founding member of the Rideau Historical Society. My wife and I have, over a long period of time, appreciated and lent our skills and interests to learning about and preserving the heritage we have grown up in and been part of.
There is, however, another dimension which is awfully important to me. I am probably one of the very few Members of Parliament ever to have lived for an extended period of time in a railway station. In 1942, my mother became the station manager in Glengarry, Nova Scotia. I lived in that railway station from 1942, until I started university several years later. There are a number of unique things about that. First is the fact that my mother was appointed station master in the early days of World War II. It was very unique for the Canadian National Railway to have done that.
The building was beautiful. It was in large part a two-storey building, gabled windows in the upper storey, a freight shed with a flat roof, a waiting room about twice the size of the entrance to the West Block, with a fully functional telegraph office. It was simply a beautifully designed building, very, very functional, serving two main functions. One was to serve a prosperous rural community in the highlands of Nova Scotia, and the other was as a landmark on the railway line between New Glasgow and Truro where there was a break in the long grade over Gordon Summit crossing the height of land across Nova Scotia.
I would remind those who are not familiar with that area that the heaviest grades on railway lines in Canada exist on that branchline. That plateau on the railway line, the break in grade, served as a point for hooking on extra engines to get over the grade. It was important to the service of the local community and it was important in the functioning of the railway line.
The tragedy of all that, as I look back now at that magnificent structure, is that it is no longer there. In fact, if you drive by where that magnificent old building stood, a building which meant so much to me in my boyhood but, more important, so much to that great agricultural community in northern Nova Scotia, it has simply been destroyed. With that has gone an awful lot of railway history in Nova Scotia and a big part of that community.

As a professional geologist it has been my pleasure to travel widely in Canada over the years. The adoption of this Bill will ensure that three railways stations, which I consider to be great, will be preserved. The first I want to make mention of is the railway station in Cobalt, Ontario, owned by the Ontario Northland Railway. I do not know how many of my colleagues in the House have seen that station. It is a simply magnificent building and I hope it will fall under the purview of this Act. Another is the railway station in Whitehorse owned and operated by the Yukon and White Pass Railway. It is again a magnificent historical building which is linked very closely to the heritage of Canada. The third one of which I want to make note is the CPR station in Smiths Falls. It as well is a beautiful building architecturally and is very important to the evolution of the railway community in eastern Ontario.
In offering these comments I want to express my thanks to the Member for Bow River, to those colleagues of ours who served on the legislative committee, and to all Members of the House for their co-operation in adding a dimension to Canada's heritage in order that those who follow us will benefit from a great era in the evolution of Canada. So much of our historic economic evolution is related to railways and it should be a great priority for us to enhance that remembrance.

That Bill C-139 be amended in Clause 90 by striking out lines 44 at page

"(b) $4,675 plus 23 per cent of the amount by".
He said: Mr. Speaker, the objective of Motion No. 7 is to reduce from 26 to 23 per cent the middle tax rate for taxpayers with taxable incomes between $27,500 and $55,000. The rate structure would then be 17, 23, and 29 per cent, which would be much fairer than the one proposed by the Government.

Mr. Speaker, as I just said in English, the purpose of this motion is to reduce the middle tax rate for taxpayers with a taxable income between $27,500 and $55,000 from 26 per cent to 23 per cent. The rate structure would therefore be 17, 23 and 29 per cent which would be much fairer than the Government 's proposal.
Mr. Speaker, I would have preferred to table a different kind of amendment that would probably have added an additional tax rate. However, this would not be allowed under our Standing Orders, at this stage, and I am sure the Chair would have declared the amendment out of order at this stage of the proceedings. As you know, amending a tax Bill is not the easiest thing in the world because of the precedents and financial questions involved, and the Standing Orders of the House leave us very little leeway. The only thing I could do at this stage was to suggest a drop in the middle tax rate from 26 per cent to 23 per cent.
August 25, 1988

Mr. Speaker, the tax reform has changed the number of tax rates we had so far.

The Government has decided to reduce the number of tax brackets from ten to three. If this amendment is defeated, the federal rate will be 17 per cent on the first $27,500 of taxable income, 26 per cent for the additional dollars between $27,500 and $55,000, and 29 per cent on all income over $55,000.
We believe that three tax brackets are not enough. Had the rules of the House allowed me to do so I would have introduced a more complex amendment. It is not, however, possible for me to do that. I tabled this amendment in order to have the opportunity to express my point of view on the number of rates of taxation. As I have said before, three rates do not produce a progressive type of taxation.
We also believe that the gap between the second and the third rate is not large enough. It is amazing that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) decided to impose a 17 per cent tax on the first $27,000 and then jump nine points from 17 per cent to 26 per cent. There is another increase for additional earnings, but only of three percentage points. That is certainly not enough and I think that is unfair for the middle class. When we compare the taxes that middle class Canadians will pay after tax reform with the dollars they were paying in 1984 we see that the average family will have a burden of more than $1,200 per year. We say that this situation is completely unacceptable and we think it should be amended.

Mr. Speaker, when we take a closer look at the situation in various income groups, we see that according to the new tax table proposed by the Minister of Finance, with the new tax rates, people with an income of $27,000 or $28,000 will see their additional earnings.. . Someone with an income of $28,000 who has two children will see his additional earnings, say he has a raise of $1,000, this pay increase will be taxed at a marginal rate that is higher than for people with an income of $100,000. The reason is quite simple. At this income level, when you get a pay raise of $1,000, your child tax credit is reduced by 5 per cent, so that your actual tax rate is not 26 per cent but 26 per cent plus 5 per cent or 31 per cent-2 per cent more than for the person who earns $100,000 and gets a pay increase of $1,000.
This person will have to pay 29 per cent federal income tax on the additional $1,000. However, the other person who has a family with two children and whose income would increase from $28,000 to $29,000 would pay 31 per cent on the additional $1,000.
That is why we say this tax reform is unfair to families, something that has been repeated ad nauseam by all witnesses who appeared before the Finance Committee.
There are people who will say, and I am sure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is one of them, that we don't have enough money to do something that will cost more than $1 billion. I would like to point out to the Minister that the main

reason he got into this fix in the first place is that he wanted to introduce tax reform in two stages, the first stage before the election and the next stage after the election, and this remedy or, should I say, this lack of courage, is being paid for by the middle class whose income will be taxed at 26 per cent, while wealthier groups might see their additional income taxed at a lower rate.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore move this amendment, and I trust it can be considered in accordance with our Standing Orders and will reflect the objective 1 have in mind which is to make it quite clear that the tax reform proposed by the Minister of Finance is unfair to families. If the Minister of Finance tells me they don't have enough money and that one billion dollars is too rich for the Government, I say now, before he has a chance to give me that argument, that I find this very hard to believe, coming from a Minister and a Government that is prepared to invest $10 billion in nuclear submarines.
If the Minister has any other points to make, I would be glad to hear them. But I will say that personally, if 1 had the resources and if our Standing Orders had allowed me to table a more complex amendment, I would have preferred to add a tax rate, because 1 still believe and 1 am convinced that three rates are not enough and that we should probably have 17, 23, 26, 29 and 31 per cent. 1 pointed out earlier and explained why at this stage of the debate, the Standing Orders do not allow me to do that, and I used the little leeway I had to make it clear to the House that there was a problem here that we had to solve.
I said a moment ago that middle class families will pay an effective marginal rate that will be superior to the marginal rate of taxation for people earning over $100,000.
The Senate Standing Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce, in its report on tax reform, calculated the real rate. These vary according to the number of dependent children and family income level. The following example has been calculated for a family with two children. What I said a moment ago about the marginal rate of 31 per cent is very well demonstrated in this report by the Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce that was tabled in the other place.
I have read the report and am convinced that they are perfectly right that for everyone with an income between $27,500 and $45,000, the marginal rate will be 31 per cent if they have two children. That is unfair for the middle class and I hope the Government will accept this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's proposal is to reduce the middle income marginal tax rate from 26 per cent to 23 per cent. When I looked at the motion, I asked myself what would be the revenue implications. They are rather horrendous, at some $1.8 billion. That alone encourages one to look very closely at this proposal.

August 25, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
The other day we discussed the automobile question with the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau). This is very much a limousine Liberal kind of motion. It ends up indulging the upper middle class at the expense of the lower middle class income tax bracket in absolutely grotesque proportions.
The tax rate under $27,500 would be the same as that proposed in the tax reform. However, from $27,500 to $55,000, the Liberals would reduce the marginal tax rate from 26 per cent to 23 per cent. That is the federal rate.
In order to understand how grotesque this proposal is, let us assume a 55 per cent provincial tax rate and combine it with the federal tax rate. Those rates would be 26.35 per cent for under $27,500; 40.3 per cent for the $27,500 to $55,000 bracket; and 44.95 per cent for $55,000 and over.
Let us review the tax savings at various income levels as a result of the proposal of the Hon. Member. I would like the Hon. Member's response to these because they concern every Canadian. First, the tax savings he would turn over to those at the income level of $27,000 as a result of his so-called improvement would be zero. At $30,000 it would be $75 federal, $115 federal-provincial combined if we assumed the 55 per cent provincial tax rate. That is a 0.4 per cent change as a percentage of income, a very small step forward for the $30,000 income Canadian.
Let us look at the $40,000 income level taxpayer. The combined federal-provincial savings would be $580 according to his proposal, which is a 1.5 per cent change as a percentage of income.
At $55,000, it would be a combined federal-provincial savings of $1,275 in tax, which is a 2.3 per cent change as a percent of income.
This would not only cost the Government of Canada and the Consolidated Revenue Fund $1.8 billion, a massive haem-morrhage on the Treasury, it would be horrendously regressive within the middle income tax category. It would provide no benefit to low income filers. Lower middle income filers would receive a small tax reduction from the proposal, while upper middle and high income filers would be the major beneficiaries. That is the import of this proposal.
The marginal tax rate that is proposed in Bill C-139 provides a much better balance of tax reductions to Canadians, while respecting fiscal constraint. Tax reform respects fiscal restraint and comes to terms with constantly trying to reduce the federal government deficit. When we consider the middle income category, we can see that it is progressive.
The Hon. Member's suggestion is regressive. It is a limousine Liberal approach to the middle class.
