The Progressive Conservative tax regime gives the greatest tax concessions since 1984 to whom? Does it give it to senior citizens, pensioners or families trying to scrape by on $300 or $400 a week? No. It gives the greatest concessions to people earning over $100,000 a year.
1 have a Summary for Taxpayers, a booklet that was prepared by the Department of Finance. It has a little "Canada" with a blue thing over the top of it for the flag. It was changed from red. The booklet points out that for households with a decrease in tax, families under $15,000 in income will get an average reduction of $140. Families earning under $30,000 will receive a cut of $460. Families earning in the range of $30,000 to $50,000 will receive an average cut of $525. Families in the $50,000 to $100,000 range, among those with a decrease in tax, will receive a cut of $735. The result, Mr. Speaker, is that only families and taxpayers with an income of over $100,000 a year will pay less tax in 1988, after tax reform, than they paid in 1984, when the Progressive Conservative Party came to power.
Mr. Speaker, all other families will pay more tax, although slightly reduced by tax reform, but the net result is a tax increase if you count the sales tax and other taxes raised by the Conservatives.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in real terms, the average family is suffering under Conservative rule. Its purchasing power is much less in 1988, than it was in 1984. Mr. Speaker, this is mainly due to the Government's piling tax upon tax on the average family and the average taxpayer.
Mr. Speaker, 1 do not fully agree with the Liberal Party's amendment, but what my friend from Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) has suggested is specifically to change the tax rates for middle-income individuals, who are the base of the tax system. He is proposing that the marginal rate be reduced from 26 per cent to 23 per cent.
To begin with, Mr. Speaker, I wonder why, under the Conservatives' tax reform, a technician working for Bell Canada, for example, or an operator taking telephone calls who earns maybe $28,000 or $29,000 a year pays a marginal federal income tax rate of 26 per cent, while at the same time Jean de Grandpre, the president and CEO, the big chief of that company, with an income of over a million dollars a year, only pays a marginal rate of 29 per cent. Is that a real difference?
So here you have someone with an annual income of over $1 million who only pays the federal Government a marginal rate of 29 per cent. But the technician or the lady who takes telephone calls and works all sorts of hours, who is now on strike because of Bell Canada's effort to deny her a proper standard of living, pays a marginal rate that differs by only 3 per cent, i.e. 26 per cent.

What the Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Hockin) just said is unacceptable, Mr. Speaker. Rather than come up with sound reasons and explain its position on that, the Government wonders how much that will cost, Mr. Speaker. Is this the way to go about achieving tax reform? This is not tax reform. It is adjusting the Income Tax Act to the Government's needs.
In the United States, Mr. Speaker, when the Americans decided to go into tax reform, it worked because all parties agreed on the mechanisms, the principle of that tax reform. They set up their parameters and told the officials: Here they are, implement them. There was no question of looking at costs only. Do we build up society by looking at the costs or by having principles of social fairness? This afternoon, we have clear and specific evidence that this Government has no idea of what social justice is, what fairness to all is.
Mr. Speaker, they always end up talking about money each time we come up with a proposal for child care services, which everyone has come to need. Each time we come up with proposals to lighten the tax burden of senior citizens, the answer is there is no money. But money they have, Mr. Speaker, to buy nuclear submarines. Will that bring us social justice? This shows the Conservative Party for what it really is. What my colleague for Laval-des-Rapides is proposing is very simple.
But the Minister of State (Finance) argued this would increase costs. Therein lies his error, Mr. Speaker, and I will not elaborate because this is so technical it might be difficult to explain to Canadians. What my colleague for Laval-des-Rapides is asking for is a change in rates, not the basic amount. This is what the Minister would not understand. What do we propose? We propose to reduce the rate from 26
per cent to 23 per cent, the average tax rate, for taxpayers with taxable income between $27,500 and $55,000. This is clear and simple. We are looking for social justice between the 17 per cent and the 29 per cent. Is that clear enough? The tax structure would include tax rates of 17 per cent, 23 per cent, and 29 per cent, which would be much more equitable than that proposed by the Government.
I spent two full days sitting on the Finance Committee, and whenever we proposed something ... I remember that one night, the Conservatives Members on the Committee were fully in agreement with me and we removed one of the clauses-more on that later-but then we had to recant when an official commented that the proposal was impossible to accept because it would cost too much money. Yet, when we had discussed it without any reference to the costs, even the Tory Members were in agreement. But when faced with the costs, they said: "Hold everything!" That is what the so-called tax reform is all about, Mr. Speaker! It's really a joke to talk about tax reform when taxpayers are not treated fairly and when the only reason for amending the Income Tax Act is to make it possible for the Government to get other revenues while lulling Canadians taxpayers into believing that it is easing their tax burdens.

It was so unfair that once you got beyond having a couple of children you would actually be worse off under tax reform than you would have been without it. That certainly seemed like a perverse situation. That is why the Government decided that it would increase the child tax credit for the third or subsequent child.
1 believe that the amendment extends that to a dependant aged 19 to 21. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) will talk about that. However, there is something more generally perverse about the Government's proposal. Take a couple of people in similar circumstances, say Joe and Jim or Mary and Sue who all work for Revenue Canada. Each one is a bread-winner. Each has comparable circumstances as far as the family is concerned and each is aged 31 or 32. Joe has a wife and couple or three kids. His seat-mate, the person working right next to him, Jim, has the same job with the same income, but instead of having children he is putting money into RRSPs to the maximum allowable according to government policy. Anybody would assume that the wage earner with the family would be treated more generously than the wage earner with the RRSP deduction, but it is the contrary under the Conservatives. I think there is something wrong with that.

August 25, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
The Government shows that it has its values turned around. If the Government were really concerned about the family, which I believe will be an important issue in the forthcoming election campaign, it would not have to bring in these artificial amendments about the third and subsequent child and so on. The Government would have demonstrated a commitment to equity by ensuring that the tax system in this country genuinely aided people with family responsibilities. Tax systems are there to raise revenue, but they also are there to express a social philosophy about the kind of society and the kind of country we want to have. Conservative tax philosophy does not have a great deal to say about the men and women, the parents who are raising kids in our society. I get upset over that, Mr. Speaker, as I get upset when I find developers and entrepreneurs in my constituency open up what they call adult only apartment buildings. My constituents who have children find they are shut out of desirable accommodation because it is adult only. I would have thought that everybody in society should have a commitment, but the Conservatives do not seem to have that.
1 want to comment specifically on Motion No. 8 which aims to substitute full indexing for the deindexation put forward by the Minister of Finance in his tax reform proposals. It is very interesting to think that the Conservatives have come full circle on this question of indexing. You will recall that it was the Conservatives under Robert Stanfield who proposed that the tax system be indexed, some time back in the late 1960s. They fought for that and they thought it was fair. The New Democrats thought it was fair as well. Finally, ironically, it was the then Minister of Finance, the now Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner), who brought indexing into the tax system.
My Party still supports indexing, particularly for people with modest incomes. I know where Robert Stanfield was on this issue and I know where the Conservatives are now. They have turned full face. They have abandoned the commitment they made in the 1960s and the 1970s. Now, instead of full indexation, it is indexation minus 3 per cent.
This is a very subtle way to impose a tax increase on average Canadians year after year. The child tax credit is partially deindexed. The value goes down by 3 per cent every year. The family allowance is partially deindexed. The value goes down by 3 per cent every year in any year when the rate of inflation exceeds 3 per cent.
The tax reform brackets are only partially deindexed, and therefore, rather than rising with inflation, they decline in value every year. That means that for people who are sitting around those turning points there is an increase in taxation every year. It is a hidden increase in taxation and, therefore, it is a dishonest increase in taxation.
I suppose that the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) will tell us that the $100,000 limit on tax-free capital gains is totally deindexed, that it will be worth $100,000 next year, the year after that, and the year after that. I suppose that is the case, but it will take an awfully long time for an average family paying these increases in taxes to catch up with the privilege given to the wealthy family who is able to take advantage of having an investment property, some stocks and bonds, or an investment in a company and make $100,000 without paying a nickel in tax on that investment. Therefore, I would say that that argument falls.
My own feeling is that we should focus the indexing and protection against inflation at people on modest incomes. In the United States, as a matter of fact, there is a procedure by which the lower rates and the lower tax brackets for people at the top of the income scale are recaptured. Once the income of an American goes above $70,000 or $80,000, he then finds himself paying additional taxes on the money in the $20,000, $30,000, or $40,000 bracket which was initially taxed at the lower rate. I do not think that that is unfair. I think that is reasonable and recognizes the fact that if there is to be some moderation of tax rates, then there should not be the additional moderation for people at the top of the income scale getting reduced rates on the first $5,000, $10,000, or $15,000 when it is taxed.
The Government has focused this particular measure on people with modest incomes. The deindexing which takes place should not be there. I believe we should have full indexing for people on modest incomes so that, as their incomes rise, in order to keep pace with the cost of living, they do not then find that the tax person has his or her hands in their pockets before they get the benefit of some protection against inflation through rising incomes.
We have seen over the last few years just what the Conservatives have done. They raised the sales tax in 1984, they raised it again, and they raised it again. They eliminated the special tax cuts that were given to families on modest incomes. They brought in tax reform which they say will take 850,000 people off the tax rolls without pointing out that they added one million people to the tax rolls beforehand. All these things are a part of a tax grab which seems to be hitting particularly at people on modest incomes.
There is a theory of taxation that says we have to hit average people because there are so many of them. I think that is to hold average people in contempt. I think average, ordinary Canadians are prepared to pay their fair share, but they do not think it is right if they are paying, and paying, and paying again because wealthy Canadians are getting a privilege, on top of a concession, on top of a loophole, on top of another new way they can avoid paying income tax. Partial deindexing is particularly offensive because it is not just a once-and-for-all kind of thing, it is a measure which will go on year after year.
August 25, 1988

It is as though the Minister of State for Finance is reaching out from his heartland in London. Long after he ceases to be a Member of Parliament, he and the Minister of Finance will still have their hands in the pockets of ordinary Canadians with this partial deindexing proposal if we do not do something about it. That is why I happen to believe that Motion No. 8, which seeks to substitute full indexing for the deindexation contained in the Finance Minister's proposal, is a good one and should be accepted.
The Minister of State for Finance might pop up and say: "Oh, you are giving a privilege to people earning over $55,000 a year because you are going to let them benefit from full indexing". I would then challenge him to come behind the curtains with me and devise a tax system which is really fair for those people earning over $55,000 per year, a system designed on the American model, perhaps, a system that would ensure that the rates paid are more appropriate, given the ability to pay.
Let us get rid of the system in which the rich get tax cuts, ordinary people get tax increases, and partial deindexing will hit average Canadians in secula saeculorum, century after century, unless we do something about it. The time to do something is now, and 1 would urge you, Mr. Speaker, to step down from your chair and join the New Democrats, and in this case their colleagues, the Liberals, in ensuring that some tax fairness is put back into tax reform.

Mr. Speaker, I want very much to have the opportunity to speak on this group of amendments, particularly those that apply to family benefits. We have to think of families in a different way than we think of single taxpayers who are concerned only with their own costs and with two wage earners who have no dependants. It is absolutely essential that we put a much greater emphasis on the needs of families, both from the point of view of the cost of raising children and from the point of view of the contribution parents with their children, the next generation, make to society for the rest of us. This is the generation that will pay for our old age pensions.
The Government has spoken a lot about being sympathetic to families, wanting to recognize families, yet the whole tax system has done the reverse. Family benefits have gone down rather than up and single taxpayers have had greater increases in tax benefits than have parents who have the extra costs and responsibilities and are contributing so much to society by raising children.
1 would like to speak particularly to Motion No. 12 which concerns child tax credits for older children, dependants who are in the age bracket of 19 to 21. There are many, many parents who still have dependent children in that age group. The Government, of course, has disregarded this and has entirely removed them from the child tax credit coverage. We are talking now about lower income families.
We are told that this is fair since the parents of those going on to post-secondary education will be able to deduct the school fees from their income tax. Of course, it is absolutely
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
essential that parents of these children are able to deduct at least these fees. There are many other costs which they will not be able to deduct. However, the Conservatives have completely disregarded a very large group of young people who are not going on to post-secondary education of any kind. They are not lucky enough to be able to get into college or university or trade training. Essentially they are at home. We must think also of parents with disabled children and the tremendous costs involved.
However, 1 would like to speak primarily about young people, many of them in my riding, who are unemployed, unable to get into training programs, and their parents have very low incomes. Many of those parents are single parents, on welfare in many cases, and they have been completely ignored by the Conservatives, and ignored in this Liberal amendment unless they happen to have two children. I do not know why they penalize the parent with one or two children. It costs quite a bit to feed them if they are at home and not working. There are many costs that their parents have to cover.
I happen to have Statistics Canada figures for the riding of Vancouver East. I would like to point out that for the age group of 15 to 24, the unemployment rate for males is 26.5 per cent; very high. For females it is a little less at 16.9 per cent. Let us compare that to 20 per cent and 15 per cent for those adults over 25. That is a very high unemployment rate, and I see that there are some 40,000 people in my riding who are not in the labour force but are over the age of 15 years.
These young people are living at home under a lot of stress. It is a time of conflict between parents and children. The young people are feeling very discouraged and worthless, and parents are feeling pretty hostile because they have to carry the expense and are barely managing to survive as it is, I am sure. It is grossly unfair and increasing the tension in families for the Government, then, to remove the child tax credit. It is kind of a last straw for poor families. I cannot understand why the Government would not cover these children and make the child tax credit available to the parents. We urge the Government to reconsider this.
Nor do we think that Motion No. 12, the Liberal amendment, is adequate. It recognizes that the child tax credit should be increased for dependants aged 19 to 21, but only if the taxpayer has three or more dependants. I do not know why they put that restriction on it. It seems very unfair. Certainly poor families that I know of cannot manage with two children. The alternative for these young people is to go on welfare. As my colleague says, in Quebec they would only get $150 a month living out of the home. That means that they are forced on to the streets to earn additional money for survival by illicit means. It certainly happens in my riding. If they are still staying at home, their parents are penalized, and it is very difficult for young people living at home to qualify for social assistance. This in turn forces children out of the home and forces parents to tell them that if they leave home and go out on the skids at least they will get welfare; very inadequate welfare it is.

August 25, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
This policy is adding to that syndrome for welfare families, so we should not support Motion No. 12. It is a slight step in the right direction, but it discriminates against certain kinds of families with one or two dependants. We urge the Government to reconsider its tax measures in this area.

Mr. Speaker, of the amendments grouped for debate I would like to address Motion No. 10 which stands on the Order Paper in my name. It deals with the tax treatment of older dependent children, 18 and up. The (a) part of my amendment deals with older children in a one-parent family and the (b) part deals with older children in the two-parent family.
I first want to talk about the equivalent to married tax credit or tax deduction which was available before this so-called tax reform to a single parent with a dependent child under 21. The equivalent to married deduction which could be claimed by the parent in such a case has been valued by the Department of Finance at $3,740 for 1987. A single parent can no longer claim that. The Government is, instead, offering a new credit which is only available if the child is under 18. This fails to consider the 18 year old who is still at home and going to school. In Ontario the average 18 year old is still in high school. This also fails to consider the 18 year old living at home and unemployed.
For a number of years now the unemployment rate for people under 25 has been double the national average. People with high school education only have particular difficulty in getting into the labour force. In 1986, the national employment rate for 18-year-olds was 21.4 per cent; for 19, 20, and 21-year-olds it was 19.3 per cent, 18 per cent, and 16.5 per cent respectively; generally about twice the national average, twice the unemployment rate for people over 25, particularly for those who have specialized skills. Single parents who are supporting older children at home are particularly hard hit because when the child reaches 18 the family allowance cheque stops, the right to receive the child tax credit, which will be increased in 1988, stops, and for the parent who receives support from the other spouse, child support payments very often stop when the child becomes 18.
For a single parent with a low income, and it is mostly women and single parents who have custody of their children, removing access to the equivalent to married deduction for a dependent child under 21, which is, as I said, valued by the Department of Finance at $3,740 in 1987, comes at a very difficult time when other forms of support are drying up.
The Government claims that it has made up for the loss of this deduction by providing a sales tax credit of $70 to 18-year-olds regardless of their dependent status. Also there will be a tuition fee credit for the parents of youths in postsecondary education. This does nothing for the parents of
dependent youths who are either still in high school or unemployed. Clearly, the government proposal makes life harder for single parents with older dependent children. That is the purpose of my Motion No. 10 (a) which would amend Bill C-139 in Clause 92 by striking out line 49 and substituting the following therefore:
"under 21 years of age and in full-time attendance at a school or under 21 years of age and unemployed or so"
The second part of my motion deals with the older dependent child living in a two-parent family. The child who is in high school or the child who is unemployed is quite a heavy burden financially-although he or she may be a great joy in other ways-if the parents have a low income. As in the case of a single parent, family allowance benefits and the right to a child tax credit stop at age 18.
The Government argues that a credit will be available to parents with physically and mentally infirm children. This is no help to parents with healthy 18-year-olds who have to be supported in high school and whose clothing, transportation, recreation, and food bills still have to be met. It certainly is no help for the parent with an unemployed 18-year-old who also has to be provided with the necessaries to help in a job search.
In order to return some fairness to the situation, Motion No. 10 (b) would extend the current personal exemption to parents with children 21 years of age and under, regardless of the state of their health.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak to these motions because they raise some important matters of principle on which the Government should make its response clear. I would like to begin with a blanket comment about the analogy and example used by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) which seems to underpin his critique of tax reform, that is, his example of the Chairman of Bell Canada and the average Bell worker because he is concerned about progressivity. I think I can help him with his problem because he is using marginal tax rates instead of average tax rates. If he took average tax rates he would feel better about the progressivity of our system.
I will given an example. If you take the combined federal and provincial rate, under tax reform a one-earner couple earning $30,000 with two children has a 13.7 per cent average tax rate. I think the Hon. Member knows what an average tax rate is. It is different from a marginal tax rate which is the tax on the next dollar when you move into a new bracket. The average tax rate is what you actually pay on an income of $30,000.
August 25, 1988

On $60,000 the average tax rate is 29.2 per cent. On $100,000 the average tax rate is 35.8 per cent. Once again, I am talking about combined federal and provincial taxes. The average tax rate on $200,000 is 40.8 per cent. I have no idea whether Mr. de Grandpre earns $1 million a year, but if so he would be taxed at a 44.8 per cent average tax rate.
The system is very strongly progressive when you use average tax rates which, of course, is the rate you should look at. We all know that when we do our taxes we think the marginal tax rate is high, but when we work it out we see that it is somewhat less because the average turns out to be less. It is the average ladder which is really the measure of a tax system progressivity. The Member is misunderstanding tax reform because he misunderstands the difference between marginal and average tax rates.
The Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) and the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) have brought motions before the House as well this evening and 1 would like to respond to those. First, the implications of removing the indexing restrictions of the CPI minus three for the refundable child tax credit and the disability credit, from a point of view of revenue, are not trivial. This would cost $75 million.
Allow me to speak to this proposal. Over recent years the Government has introduced a number of changes increasing the benefits of both the refundable tax credit and the disability credit. The general problem that 1 have with all these Liberal motions is that they take one little piece out of the mosaic and look at it rather than looking at the whole mosaic.
I remind Members that we have been increasing benefits under the refundable tax credit and the disability credit. The child tax credit was increased by $70 in 1986, and by $35 in 1987-88. Tax reform further increased the refundable child tax credit by $35 in 1988. The new child care initiatives also increase the refundable child tax credit by $100 in 1988, and by $200 in 1989, and subsequent taxation years for children under seven years of age without child care receipts.
This is all part of the story. This Liberal motion conveniently overlooks these very important parts of the mosaic which makes up the tax system of Canada after tax reform. As a result of the combination of these changes, many parents with children under seven years of age will benefit from a $375 increase in the refundable child tax credit. It must be said in this House over and over again that all these credits end up being much more beneficial than the restriction on the CPI minus three about which Hon. Members opposite complain.
The new disability credit, too, is more advantageous than the old exemption for the majority of beneficiaries. The credit is worth $550, while the old exemption of $29.20 was worth $496 for someone with income of less than $27,500. There, too, the system is more generous and better targeted. The House should know that as a result of the change introduced
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
by the Government in 1986, 85,000 new disabled persons have benefited from the expansion of the criteria of eligibility.
Motion No. 9 would increase from $500 to $1,000 the amount of income that a spouse may earn before the credit for marital status is reduced, and Motion 11 would do the same in the case of the equivalent to married credit. I want to speak to that, another motion which would cost the federal Treasury $75 million.
We do not feel that this is the way to go because, first, the $500 is the exempt income threshold under the existing law. It is important that we understand that increasing this amount would simply open the door to increased income splitting between high income spouses with income from property and non-working spouses. We just do not believe that this is fair. We thought about this very carefully and did not want to stand on the side of unfairness with regard to this.
The increase in the value of the marital credit provided in tax reform increases by over $1,200, from $4,300 to $5,500, the amount of income that may be earned before the relief for married status ends up being reduced to zero. This makes sense. This is clearly the way to approach tax reform. It does not make sense to accept this motion and incur an extra $75 million from the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
Motion No. 10 (a) extends the equivalent to married exemption for children aged 19 to 21 who are in full-time attendance at school or unemployed. The Hon. Member for Trinity spoke to this and I would like to deal with it. This, too, would cost around $75 million. Let us understand the history and all that surrounds this. Prior to tax reform the equivalent to married exemption could be claimed by a taxpayer who was single, divorced, separated, or widowed who supported a dependant of any age living with him or her during the year.
Under tax reform, the equivalent to married exemption has been converted into an equivalent to married credit. The credit can be claimed for a parent or grandparent of the taxpayer, an infirm relative, or a dependant 18 years of age or younger. Let us remember that we have broadened what we mean by dependant.
The Hon. Member for Trinity expressed concern for those between the ages of 19 and 21. Things have changed in this country. Previously, the age of majority was 21 but it has been reduced over time, and age 18 is now generally regarded as the age of majority for most federal laws and programs and most provincial family laws and social assistance programs. Would the pages want us to raise the age of majority to 21? Does it not make sense that it is at age 18? This has been done at the provincial level as well as at the federal level. For example, both the family allowance and the Canadian and Quebec Pension Plans regard age 18 as the upper limit for minor children.

August 25, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
There could have been a misunderstanding in this debate. We must remember that children who turn 18 in a year will continue to benefit from the refundable child tax credit, the dependent child credit, as well as the equivalent to married credit. Dependants 19 and over in full-time attendance at a post-secondary school will be able to transfer the unused portion of up to $600 of the education and tuition credits to a supporting spouse, parent, or grandparent. This represents a significant improvement over the existing system for children in post-secondary schools.
Recently 1 talked to a group of university presidents who said that this was very helpful. Again, the pages must appreciate this proposal. That deduction used to have to be taken by the low income earning student. Now it can be transferred to a parent or grandparent who could get more benefit from it.
The suggested increase to age 21 would set a wholly arbitrary age restriction. Those are basically my problems with the motion by the Elon. Member for Trinity. We have a new age of majority, we have the unused tuition fees credit, we have dependents 19 and over who can claim the refundable sales tax credit in their own right. This means that it would be inconsistent for the tax system to treat a 19 to 21 year old person as two things: a dependent child and as an adult. It is one or the other. This system treats them as an adult.
All these measures add up to a significant improvement over the existing system for children in post-secondary schools. Furthermore, children turning 18 in a year will continue to benefit from the refundable child tax credit, the dependent child credit, as well as the equivalent to married credit. Tax reform provides a $250 tax credit for older children who are dependent by reason of mental or physical infirmity.
The burden of my intervention this evening is to say that we should not look at one piece of tax reform and criticize it, try to increase it or make it more liberal. We should consider the whole mosaic to see the fairness of tax reform, the useful targeting of tax reform, and the progressivity of it as well. [Translation]

Madam Speaker, I would like to talk about this group of motions, but especially about Motion No. 8. Of course, the main purpose of tax reform and of any tax system is fairness. The tax system takes money for the Government to distribute and match with those who need it. Also tax reform and tax policy give indications as to how we want our society to go.
Of course, I am thinking of several studies and I am sure that most or maybe all Hon. Members will agree that we have a demographic problem; everyone is concerned about what will happen in future with fewer children being born, the declining birth rate and all the problems related to the aging population.
So we need a family policy and it is clear that the reason we in the Liberal Party, the Official Opposition, have to propose amendments is because this Government's tax reform has completely overlooked the family. There is no incentive for the family. How can one have a tax reform and not think of indexing the refundable credits for dependent children? We talk about dependent children. We talk about the family. If we
want to encourage the family, we have only to take the latest Quebec provincial budget as an example. The Liberal Finance Minister understood that a fiscal policy on the family was required and everyone applauded this budget. Here this Government has an ideal opportunity with tax reform-we do not have tax reform every year-but it has completely missed this opportunity. Definitely, the situation for mentally and physically handicapped dependent children is incredible! How can they not index those credits? Any Government of whatever stripe that neglects this aspect is not honest.
Of course, we just heard the Minister whose whole argument was based on the question of cost. Such a motion would cost so many millions, another motion so many millions, and of course we cannot afford it, the Government does not have the money for it. However, Madam Speaker, I do not want to come back to the submarine issue, I do not want to repeat myself, but there are other expenses the Government is committed to. On military expenses, for example, it spent $2.7 million to change the military uniforms. This money could have been spent for families and social justice. Has the $41 million for the prison in Port-Cartier helped families?
When we talk about money, let us put things in their true perspective. The capital gains exemption of $500,000 announced in 1986 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) cost the federal treasury $800 millions in 1987. If we want to put things in their proper perspective, let us do it right. Let us be honest: this Government has no family policy. Family is not one of its concerns. If they could tell us what their family policy is all about, maybe we could understand them better, but they don't have any. That is why we have to propose amendments, just as we have been doing since this afternoon, proposing amendments to the child care Bill, amendments to make the tax rate fairer. We are moving amendments to index the tax credit for dependent children, for children over 18 years old, for physically handicapped children, and the Minister still talks about costs. We could spend all night talking about expenditures, and about the money this Conservative Government has been wasting for the past four years.
Madam Speaker, even if they want to make you believe that they have reduced the deficit, later, in one of my motions, I will prove that they have not reduced it at all. They want to make us think that they are reducing the deficit, but after wringing more than $25 billion in extra taxes from taxpayers, they have still not really reduced the deficit because the figures they quote come from an accounting system that they changed to make it look like they reduced the deficit, but in fact, the real deficit still there in spite of $22 billion in tax increases over four years.
Madam Speaker, on this point, I would just like to tell the House that I support Motion No. 8, as well as all the other motions grouped together that come from my colleagues, because I believe that we do need a clear and precise family policy so Canadians can know where we are going and what we have set for Canadian families.
August 25, 1988

Motion No. 13
That Bill C-139 be amended in Clause 92 by adding immediately after line
47 at page 229 the following:
"1.1) The personal income tax credit established by subsection (1) is
refundable."
Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague from Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) for supporting this motion.
Madam Speaker, this motion amending Clause 92 of Bill C-139 is aimed at bringing to the attention of the Members of this House what I think is a very important issue.
The whole idea of tax reform, we were told, was to bring a greater measure of equity and social justice in our system and to ensure a better distribution of the tax burden between the various classes in our society, between the various income groups.
I have said time and again that the approach taken by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the proposals he has made are completely out of line with the objectives and the principles he himself has outlined in his White Paper on Tax Reform.
There is no relationship whatsoever between what the Minister of Finance says and what he does as far as tax reform is concerned. And an example of this is the whole matter of tax credits given to married persons, dependants, and so on.
Though tax reform was aimed, as I said, to bring a greater measure of justice and equity in our system, a taxpayer who earns a lot of money or quite a bit of money, not hundreds of thousands of dollars, but $35,000, $40,000, $45,000, can get a tax credit, thereby reducing his tax burden. But if the taxpayer is a low-income earner, he cannot get the full tax credit because his income is too low. The tax system proposed by the Minister of Finance therefore gives tax credits to those who have money, but not to those whose income is not high enough for them to pay taxes.
According to the Minister's proposition, if you do not pay income tax you are not entitled to a tax credit. If you have- Madam Speaker, would you call the Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly), to order, she has the right to take the floor in a few minutes and if she wants to speak she should first read the texts.
As things stand now, an individual who does not earn enough to pay taxes is not entitled to the tax credit-no ifs and buts, the law says so-but someone else earning a big income can claim the tax credit. So under the tax reform of the Minister of Finance a person earning a big income will get something back from the Government, but the man or woman who earns a pittance simply does not qualify for this tax credit. This is like a subsidy for people who earn a fair amount of money and a sort of negative levy against those with a limited income.
This is why in Motion No. 13 I suggest we add after line 47 of Clause 92 at page 229 that the tax credit be refundable. This way, all taxpayers regardless of earnings, but particularly those who have no money and those at the bottom of the wage scale or without any income, could at least have the same thing, the same tax credit as someone who gets $250,000 and who at that income level will claim the full credit, like a taxpayer who gets paid $40,000 or $45,000.
As I see it, the refundable tax credit is the approach the Minister of Finance should have taken in his tax reform because that would have been the only way for him to achieve the goals he outlined in his remarks when he tabled the White Paper. The problem I have with the tax reform-and we could see that for ourselves during the many weeks when the parliamentary committee heard the testimony of a number of Canadians, accountants, and what have you-is that we were told over and over again that the legislative text and the recommendations do not square with the principles which had been established by the Minister and the Conservative Government.
August 25, 1988

The purpose of my amendment therefore is to have the tax reform reflect the words of the Minister. 1 think that the refundable tax credit approach is more equitable from both a social and a tax standpoint. It would be the first step towards a kind of guaranteed minimum income which, I suggest, would be a lot fairer, much more effective, and a much better incentive to a return to the labour market than all the formulas we have now. That is something the Minister has failed to achieve with his tax reform because the wording in this piece of legislation simply does not jibe with the principles he talked about when he tabled his paper.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to quote a booklet published by the Department of Finance under the title "Tax Reform 1987: A Summary for Taxpayers". On page 5, it is stated: "The key to making the personal income tax fairer is replacing personal income tax exemptions and some deductions with tax credits. Exemptions and deductions reduce taxable income. The value of an exemption or deduction depends on an individual's tax bracket and tax rate. Tax savings are the greatest for higher-income individuals." To put it more simply, Madam Speaker, I will say that until this Government proposed to move from a system a deduction to a system of tax credit, people in higher income brackets benefited more from deductions.
Let me give you an example: Suppose that you earn a salary of $40,000, that your tax rate is, say, 30 per cent, and that you are entitled to a $3,000 deduction; because you would have to pay 30 per cent on these $3,000, you would have saved $1,000 in taxes. But if you had a salary of $15,000, with a tax rate of 10 per cent on this $3,000 deduction, you would have saved only $300 on that amount. If such is the case, how can a former Quebec Minister of Finance tell the Elouse that we moved from a system of deduction to a system of tax credit to help the affluent? On page 5 of that booklet which was distributed free of charge to all Canadians, it is clearly stated that the tax credits are the same for all. In other words, whether your income is $27,500 or $55,000 a year, your personal exemption, which is a credit, will amount to $1,020.
Until now, a taxpayer with a $27,500 income would have had a very small credit, a very small deduction, because his or her tax rate was very low, while the taxpayer with a $55,000 income would have had a very large deduction. The fine print is that a $27,500 income resulted in a $725 deduction, while a $55,000 income resulted in a $1,240 deduction, which is almost twice as much. With the tax credit system, the taxpayer with a $27,500 income and a taxpayer with a $55,000 income are both entitled to a personal $1,020 tax credit. How can the Hon. Member suggest that we are favouring the affluent and only people on higher income brackets? It is quite the contrary, Madam Speaker! The purpose of the conversion was to help lower income people.
Moreover, he said that a person must earn a lot of money to be entitled to a tax credit. What he means is that a person must earn enough money to pay taxes. But there are refundable tax credits. Even if you do not pay a single cent in income
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
tax, you are entitled to the refundable sales tax credit. All you have to do is fill in your income tax return and say: I owe no income tax, but I am entitled to a sales tax credit of $50 for every member of my family. And these $50 per person largely offset the sales tax increase that had to be brought in because there was no money to maintain existing social programs. Consequently, it is rubbish to argue that there is no equity in such a system. It is rubbish to assert that one has to earn a lot of money to get a tax credit which is refundable.
And as far as indexation is concerned, what the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou is not saying is that he is talking about a 3 per cent reduction of a cost of living indexation. In terms of old age security pensions, this meant approximately $7 a month. He is talking about millions, even billions for nuclear powered submarines but he is not saying that even if the family allowances indexation had been maintained, Canadian families would not have gained more than $2 or $3 with inflation above 3 per cent. Fortunately, the inflation rate is about 4 per cent right now. Why? Because we, the Conservatives, have had the courage to take steps which the Liberals have shied away from for decades. This is how we succeeded in cutting down the deficit, four years in a row. Moreover, we have reduced both inflation and interest rates, we have created jobs, we have put back to work 1,500,000 Canadians, 70 per cent of which are women, and 80 per cent of those jobs are full time jobs. Therefore, they can say what they want, Madam Speaker, but they have nothing to offer except a lot of eyewash.

Madam Speaker, I would like to speak to this motion because I guess I have seldom seen a motion on tax reform that is so fiscally irresponsible as this one. I choose my words carefully. This particular proposal would cost the Government of Canada $4 billion. The provinces would be matching it, and it would cost them $4 billion. This is an $8 billion proposal. It is a proposal from a kind of limousine Liberal approach that would drive the whole country to the poor house.
What happens with this proposal is that we would give a refundable personal income credit to everybody; a newborn child one day old would get it, a 12-month old child would get it, a housewife who is not going to work but can stay home all day long would get it. Everybody would get it. This particular proposal is the most fiscally irresponsible proposal that I think has ever come before the House. If in fact we ever did such a thing, we would end up hurting the very people that we want to help, that is, those who have the most difficulty economically in getting through life, the lowest incomes, because the provinces of course would cut back their social assistance.
When they found out that you had another $1,000 or whatever income, they would simply cut back their provincial assistance. This proposal costs $8 billion, but it does not even

accomplish what the Elon. Member wants it to do. 1 cannot understand the thinking behind this and I cannot believe that if that Party were in government it would ever bring it in. Why did they propose it tonight? They proposed it because they do not have any coherent ideas themselves about what they want to do in tax reform. This particular proposal would cost so much money that no matter what good ideas a government would have, they would not have the funds to dispense.
This kind of credit is not only fiscally irresponsible. It would not only refund over $1,000 annually to spouses who could stay at home or to wealthy corporate executives who do not need the money; everybody would get it. This whole notion of a progressive tax system would be fundamentally undermined by this proposal.
As I say, too, unfortunately much of the assistance that would go to lower income Canadians would simply be deducted by the provinces because of the income that would be picked up by this proposal at the federal level. To debate this much longer is to dignify a proposal which I do not think any credible economist or Minister of Finance would ordinarily recommend.
If in fact all that is meant in the motion is that the credit for dependent children should be refundable, that is not the way that the motion reads. I would remind the House that the refundable child tax credit is in place. This is the appropriate mechanism to ensure that it is properly targeted, and it has increased significantly by this Government, from $367 in 1985 to $559 in 1988, an increase of more than 50 per cent in just three years. We are targeting it.
Good economic management is to target properly, to help those who are in most need, but also to be fiscally responsible. This particular proposal does the exact opposite on both counts.

Madam Speaker,
I would just like to speak briefly to Motion No. 13. I think that the New Democratic Party supports the philosophy of refundable tax credits. We would agree that one of the more positive policies from a social point of view is the fact that the child tax credit is refundable. I am sure that this would apply with other forms of tax credits, perhaps the sales tax credit, for example, which I understand is about $50 per person. Why should that go only to people who pay income tax when it is the marginal people who do not earn enough to pay very much income tax, or those who do not earn enough to pay any income tax? Surely, they should be able to take advantage of that. It would make sense to make it refundable, so that it applies to those who do not have enough income tax to declare but still should have the benefit of the tax credit.
Another aspect to think about from a social policy point of view is that this is the beginning of the mechanism that a
number of people feel is a start on a form of guaranteed income in Canada. We very much need to find a way and a mechanism for redistributing incomes that will benefit lower income people and that will tax higher earning people at a much greater rate. By redistributing this through refundable tax credits, it would mean that lower income people would receive more.
The Minister pointed out differences between provinces and the federal Government. I think that that would be a point of negotiation to work out. Basically we are in favour of the principle of refundable tax credits.

Madam Speaker, I do not intend to make a long speech. I see that the Minister had to leave the Chamber, but there are a couple of questions that occurred to me when this question of refundable versus ordinary tax credits came up. The Minister expressed great concern that making all tax credits refundable could have the effect of costing the federal Treasury something like $4 billion, which he felt would be matched by the provincial governments. He then went on to explain that while it would cost the provincial governments in income tax, they would save a like amount through the welfare system. It is basically with the federal Government that the cost accrues.
The question that I want the House to consider a little is: If the Government, any government now or in the past or in the future, is proposing a tax credit and begins the practice of making it a refundable tax credit, will that not make governments a little more specific about why they are putting the tax credit in place in the first place?
There is not much point in pretending to have a universal tax credit for individuals for sales tax, as my colleague from Vancouver East has pointed out, if the low income people for whom the general public thought that tax credit was being put into effect could not take advantage of it. The only way that those kinds of programs make any sense is if they are refundable tax credits. What is the point of having a refundable tax credit if the bulk of the poor people do not have enough income tax against which to write off the tax credit?

Madam Speaker, the purpose of Motion No. 14 which I am proposing and which, if passed, would amend Clause 97 of Bill C-139 is to raise by $1,500 the net income threshold over which the refundable dependent child credit begins to be reduced.
In fact, this amendment seeks only to bring the income treshold back to what it was before tax reform.
Madam Speaker, once again, justice and equity are our considerations in moving this motion in an attempt to correct the approach which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and his colleague the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) have taken in this tax reform one which I can only describe as being utterly mean heedless of families' needs.
We are proposing to raise from $24,090 to $27,590 the net income threshold over which the refundable child tax credit begins to be reduced because tax reform has changed the definition of net income. It has been changed because some deductions which were allowed before and on which net income was based have been eliminated. For instance, contributions to a pension fund, to the Quebec Pension Plan, to the Canada Pension Plan for those who live in provinces other than Quebec, to unemployment insurance and the $500 employment income have all been done away with, and the definition of "net income" has thus been changed without any amendment to the legislation itself.
The normal thing to do, Madam Speaker, would be to bring the level back to what it was before. Before tax reform, married couples with children who were entitled to the refundable tax credit saw that credit diminish once their family income reached about $25,500. Under tax reform, and because of the changes introduced with regard to contributions to the Quebec Pension Plan, unemployment insurance and the $500 employment income, the child tax credit will now begin to decrease at the $24,000 treshold. Before tax reform, families earning $1,500 more than that could get the full child tax credit amounting to some $500, but after tax reform, that credit will start being reduced, not at an income level of $25,590 but of $24,000.
I think it is turning everything upside down and I hope the Hon. Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly) and the Minister of State (Finance) will at least recognize that. I don't know if the Minister has forgotten, but we have raised that issue at other times during debate and it seems that nobody wants to understand that low-income families will see their child tax credit reduced while their income is at the same level as before tax reform.

August 25, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts

I think this motion should be accepted. The net effect of the fiscal reform is that the definition of the net income for personal income tax has been changed. The contributions to the Canada Pension Plan and to unemployment insurance and the $500 exemption all disappear. The net income before and the net income after fiscal reform is not the same. The family with children who would receive the refundable child tax credit will have seen that child tax credit diminish if it has a net income of over $25,590. That will be reduced to $24,000.
This motion should be adopted. I will seek the support of all Members on both sides of the House to bring back the same level of income for those families in great need who otherwise would see their refundable child tax credit diminish at a very low personal income level.

Therefore, I ask the Government and the Conservative Members to think it over before refusing that amendment which would only bring things back to what they were before.
1 would also like to say, Madam Speaker, that with partial de-indexation of the child tax credit that the Government refused to re-index earlier, we are greatly increasing the difficulties facing Canadian families, who are hit hard by the Minister of Finance and the Conservative Government and their tax reform. The child tax credit is now de-indexed but it will be reduced to an income level which is the same as last year but has been affected by tricky changes the Minister of Finance hasn't been willing to correct so far.

Madam Speaker,
I would like to support this motion on behalf of the New Democratic Party. However, 1 wonder if the Liberals realize that they are being somewhat conservative in the level of the turning point for the child tax credit for which they are asking.
I am trying to recall the study we did almost two years ago on the reform of family benefits. If my memory serves me correctly, when we studied the amount of the child tax credit, we discovered that the Conservatives had reduced the level considerably from where it was under the Liberal regime when it actually went to average marginal families. It seems to me that if we really care about children, about struggling families, and about the one in five children in Canada who are poor, then we have to give higher priority to the family benefits that will benefit children. The child tax credit and the family allowance are the best vehicles for doing this.
The Government has deindexed by 3 per cent the family allowance and the child tax credit as well. 1 am not sure if the Liberals had maintained full indexation for the child tax credit or not. At the time of the family benefits study, we proposed that in order to bring the turning point for the child tax credit higher, the credit itself should be increased by 80 per cent. I
think that would have brought it up to where it would have been under the Liberal regime. We felt as well that it should be fully reindexed because if it is not reindexed, it then goes down progressively each year. It is very hypocritical to say that we are giving extra credits to poor families when in fact the basic child tax credit is going down in value by the 3 per cent deindexation every year.
If we care about children, and if we want to do something about child poverty, we have to give higher priority to benefits for families, particularly the child tax credit. This is one step forward. We would be more generous in that we would want an 80 per cent increase.
I believe this clause also covers the new $100 child care credit which will go to $200 in 1989. This would be available only to families with children under seven years of age and only to very low income families. As I have said many times in this House, I think any mother at home struggling to raise children will not feel that $200 recognizes the value of her work. She would much prefer a more generous child tax credit that is refundable. As well, the $200 for those parents who use informal baby-sitting arrangements is a big laugh when we think how much it costs per year for baby-sitting arrangements. Even if it is not licensed care, it is still expensive, and $200 is almost an insult.
1 do not think the Conservative Government is realistic. Conservative Members talk about families and children, but they will not do anything substantive to remove child poverty.

Madam Speaker, quite frankly, increasing in three years 50 per cent of the expenditures on any social program shows a very important priority. In fact, the child tax credit has been increased by this Government from $367 in 1985 to $559 in 1988. That is an increase of more than 50 per cent in three years.
The Liberal motion wants to increase the refundable child tax credit threshold by $1,500. The increase of $35 we have brought in for the child tax credit achieves much the same goals simply by a different means. I do not know what this motion really accomplishes.
For example, in 1988, partial child tax credit benefits will be provided to a one-earner family with two children and with an income of up to about $46,500 as compared to $45,000 for the same family under the original White Paper proposal. Moreover, these changes benefit all families who qualify for the refundable child tax credit at all income levels rather than just those whose family income is above the current threshold. This improves the progressivity of the child tax credit and the benefits system in particular and of the tax system in general.
This motion is unnecessary. I ask the House to defeat it, but I must ask another question of the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell). Perhaps she can respond to this when she speaks on the next motion, as would the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse). I hope Hon.

Members heard this. They would give, as would the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), the personal exemption credit to all Canadians, whether they had to pay tax or not. In other words, a child who has just been born would get it. A person who earns no income would get it. This would cost the Government of Canada $4 billion. I could not believe it, but they did say that. They believe in spending $4 billion that way when it would simply reduce what the provinces would end up giving because of their increased revenues. The targeting that we have achieved would be totally dissolved in essentially a fiscal haemorrhage. I ask that Hon. Members defeat this motion.

He said: The purpose of this amendment is to reduce from 12 per cent to 10 per cent the taxation rate of all small businesses.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take a few moments to speak to Motion No. 15 presented by the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau). The motion he put forward in the name of small business is certainly worth considering in those terms. However, it gets a bit more complicated than that.
Obviously our economy is all too dominated by very large enterprises which manage to do very well in comparison to small businesses. Small businesses find themselves all too often under-capitalized and forced to turn to financial institutions, particularly our chartered banks, for support. They have often found those banks in these last few years not nearly so sympathetic to their needs as has been true in the past.
Certainly small business has reason to be concerned about the tax rate. As the critic speaking on behalf of the Opposition suggested, to have the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) promise an 8 per cent rate to small manufacturing businesses, and having obtained credit in industry for doing that, and then turn around and hand them a 12 per cent rate, is only one more example of the breaking of faith which has marked the Government. It demonstrates the greediness of the Minister of Finance and his blind desire for revenue as it has been applied to small enterprises and individual taxpayers. In case after case the Minister has gone after small operators, small people, small companies, and allowed the big ones to get away with lesser payments or no payments at all.

August 25, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
That kind of economic situation would certainly justify support for this amendment. The difficulty with it for us in the NDP caucus is that the Canadian controlled private corporations to whose profits its rate reduction from 12 per cent to 10 per cent applies are characterized not by their necessarily being small businesses but by the anomaly, if you will, of being a big corporation.
There is in the nature of our corporate law something that strikes me very often as a contradiction in terms. You have a business as large as Eaton's, for example, which operates from coast to coast. It has a long history, a long and venerable history one would like to say, although I am not too sure I want to say that as a New Democrat being well aware of the labour policies of the Eaton family over the years, of being a supposedly private corporation. It has been closely held by the family and those involved with it, and because of this anomaly of corporate law it has been allowed to get away with reporting very little of its activities. This great company operates in the cities across our country. It pretends it is like a corner store. Conceivably one might argue this is the kind of private business in which the public has a limited right to know what is going on.
One could expand on this strange thing in our corporate law which allows such a company to be private in this way, but what counts is that companies such as Eaton's, which are Canadian controlled private corporations, would end up in this amendment the recipients of what is supposed to be a small business rate. Surely what is necessary if this kind of amendment is to be genuinely a small business rate, as the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides said it was, is that there must be some other quantitative measure of what is genuinely a small business.
There is a number of ways of doing that. One could use as a measurement the number of employees. A small business might be 50 or 100 employees or conceivably more than that. One could use sales as a measure, whatever the figure happens to be, some several million, perhaps. One could use this as a way of distinguishing small businesses under that level from the large ones over it which one would not want to call small businesses.
Clearly there are a number of objective standards that could be applied, and I have no doubt that the Department of National Revenue would have the information at hand or be able to obtain it in order to draw these distinctions. If there is any difficulty in getting it from some of these private corporations, it is quite, quite timely to ensure that they report in the way that American companies have to report information to the authorities. We should long since have done that with Canadian corporations which have gone beyond this charade, I would say, of supposed private corporations. If the law has to be amended to get us some information, it might only have to be filed with Revenue Canada. It would not have to be published for all those who are concerned to protect the privacy of these supposed private enterprises.
Those are the kinds of concerns we feel about this particular amendment. We clearly want to support that part of it which is relevant to small business. The fact that it has the wrong qualifications in it with respect to Canadian controlled private corporations leaves us much more ambivalent. In the context of the votes this evening on division, of course it is not going to matter actually how we come down on this, but it is a motion which clearly is useful in spirit but should have been far more carefully drawn in the actual letter of the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, 1 listened very carefully to the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) because of a number of questions posed in this House by his Party complaining about the number of corporations in Canada that do not pay tax. Do you remember those questions, Mr. Speaker? Tonight he is saying that we should lessen the tax burden on small business. The Hon. Member has admitted tonight that in fact most of the corporations which do not pay tax are small businesses struggling to get under way. When he asks me in the future about corporations that do not pay tax I will remind him that what he said tonight is a contradiction to all the questions he asked previously.
More important is the actual motion itself. I can deal with it very quickly. First, the 12 per cent small business rate is one of the most generous in the industrialized world. If you compare with other countries you will find that this rate is as low as you can find almost anywhere in the top 30 countries in the OECD. Therefore, we are taxing our small businesses at a very generously low rate.
Why not 10 per cent instead of 12 per cent? This proposal would cost the Consolidated Revenue Fund about $25 billion. There are a lot of things that can be done with those funds.
Third, and most important, is the point which the Hon. Member made, with which I agree, that all corporations, on the first $200,000 of revenue, would be taxed at a lower rate. That would help the large corporations as well as the small ones.
It is a Liberal motion.
It is a Liberal motion which you are supporting.
No, no, we are equivocal about it.

With regard to why we are leaving it at 12 per cent, the House will be interested to know that the rate of the dividend tax credit has been reduced under tax reform from one-third to one-quarter. This amount integrates perfectly with the 12 per cent corporate tax rate so as to ensure that corporate income that is subject to taxation at the small business rate is not taxed inordinately heavily as it is distributed by way of dividends to the shareholder. If the small business rate was to be reduced to 12 per cent, the dividend tax credit should also be reduced, otherwise too great a credit will be available.
August 25, 1988

Thus, the total tax on income, flowed through a corporation, would be less than tax on the shareholder if he earned the income directly. We are keeping the 12 per cent in order to ensure that these two are in balance and symmetry. Reducing the dividend tax credit further than has already been done by tax reform would have extensive repercussions in the public capital markets.
Once again, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) has proposed an amendment which moves in a contradictory direction to what even he intended.

Mr. Speaker, this motion proposed by the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) and the motion that 1 presented, which was ruled out of order, are meant to correct the injustice that the tax reform proposed by the Conservative Government does to small business.
So far, we had a tax system that allowed manufacturing companies a lower tax rate; there was a reduced tax rate for large manufacturing companies and a reduced rate for small manufacturing companies. Even the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), when he first presented his corporate tax reform, maintained this differential treatment and then proposed a reduced tax rate for small manufacturing companies, 8 per cent instead of 10 per cent. So the Minister of Finance wanted to continue along the same lines as we have for decades in Canada.
Since tax reform, the Minister of Finance has changed completely. Instead of continuing the tax reduction for small manufacturing companies, he increased the rate by 2 per cent. It is the only sector in the whole tax reform that is hit with a direct tax increase. Also keep in mind that this sector is hit by the lower capital cost allowance. The CCA was reduced across the board, so it applies to small business as well.
When the Minister says that the Conservative Government was generous to small business by increasing its tax rate 2 per cent, I would like him to define what he means by generosity for us. It is the only sector hit with a tax increase under tax reform. It is the only sector that creates more than 80 per cent of our jobs. Why then penalize the sectors which make the economy thrive? Is that good leadership? It is this unfair treatment of a sector which provides most of our jobs that we wanted to eliminate. Because the Standing Orders of the House prevented us from proceeding as we intended, we had to resort to this amendment in order to deal with the issue.
Mr. Speaker, we submitted this issue to the Finance and Economic Affairs Committee and once again we were given the same answer. We are told that we are too generous. Today I am asking the Finance Minister again to increase by 2 percent the small manufacturing businesses tax rate. Is that
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
too generous? Is that excessive generosity? I am sure that the small businesses will remember that come the next elections!

Mr. Speaker, we cannot possibly have the question now, I have not yet had the time to make my contribution in this debate. I am hoping that my words will influence the Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly), to change her position in favour of the right one which is the one we are suggesting.
I want to compliment the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), and I say that in a totally objective and non-partisan manner, in my usual way.
We could do even better than this, we could withdraw this amendment and ask the Government to do the right thing, that is, lower income tax for small businesses. However, we on this side of the House know that the Conservatives do not have a tendency to assist small businesses because they are too busy assisting big businesses. That is the nature of being a Tory and I accept that. My colleague from Laval-des-Rapides very astutely recognized that and proposed an amendment, the purpose of which is to lower that level of taxation.
My colleague wants to do this for a very simple reason. The current rate of income tax for general business is 36 per cent. Under tax reform that is reduced to 28 per cent. That sounds like something to applaud. If you group everyone together the rate is lowered by 8 per cent. That sounds good. However, the catch is that for small business in manufacturing the rate goes from 10 per cent to 12 per cent. Would you believe that the rate is actually going up from 10 per cent to 12 per cent under the Conservative administration? I do not want to belabour the point because my colleague from Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano), who is an expert in small business, has spoken very eloquently on this, as has my colleague from Laval-des-Rapides.
Given the constructive input I have just made, I hope the Government will agree with us and will vote in favour of the Liberal amendment.
As for the New Democratic Party, which is ambivalent about how it will vote, according to its words, I hope it will reconcile itself to vote for one side or the other. I hope they choose the right side, the Liberal side.

He said: Mr. Speaker, for the past two years, the Conservative Government has been using all the means at its disposal to make us believe it is reducing the deficit, when it is actually using a different accounting system to fool Canadians, so that when it says it is reducing the deficit, it is not doing that at all.
Mr. Speaker, for starters, the first measure accelerated the remittance of source deductions. As a result, the Minister was able to assemble the sum of $2 billion, just once, and subsequently, we were shown a drop of $2 billion in the deficit, while in fact there had been no reduction in expenditures or increase in revenue. It was just that one time when, instead of getting the money before April 15, it came in before March 31, so the Minister had $1 billion more in his fiscal year.
Mr. Speaker, the following year we got the accelerated remittance of federal sales tax. A nightmare for small businesses, Mr. Speaker, because every month the remittance must be made by estimating what the sales tax will be, and then the following month, the books have to be reconciled to calculate the exact difference-add and substract! Imagine, Mr. Speaker, the kind of nightmare this is for small businesses!
How can the Government say it is concerned about this sector? We have just considered a motion to increase income tax for small businesses.
The Government's tax reform is going to take money out of the pockets of low-income Canadians and senior citizens, with their modest pension and investment income, Mr. Speaker!
So what is the Government suggesting? The Government wants to change quarterly remittances. Everybody look at the calendar! According to us, the first quarter is up to the end of March. From now on, according to the Canadian Government, it will be until March 15, so two weeks early. Mr. Speaker, this was how they got another billion dollars to reduce the deficit, although they don't reduce anything because they just collect $1 billion two weeks early.
But we have to take into account the fact that for the Government, the fiscal year ends on March 31, and each time it announces early remittances, and it invariably does so before March 31, the Government can claim a reduction in the deficit, but this is simply not the case because all it is is a change in accounting rules.
But here, we are not dealing with source deductions, held by employers and deducted from employee paycheques or sales
tax to be remitted. That would simply involve accounting methods of working capital.
This time, Mr. Speaker, we are talking about taking money out of taxpayers pockets, from those who need it the most. I am sure that senior citizens come to see you too, Mr. Speaker, in your constituency office with their quarterly form that they do not understand, while the Government is charging $1.29 interest because they sent it in a day late, after attempting to figure out their year-end remittance and finally losing everything. Can you imagine that they must now get used to paying remittance on March 15, June 15 and September 15 instead of at the end of the month? Why, Mr. Speaker? Not too long ago, last week in fact, we had that same debate in the House and before officials of the Finance Department could figure out how much that measure would cost, even Conservative Members said that we could not possibly do such a thing to our senior citizens! As if it were not enough to try to reduce their pensions, we now want to pick their pockets.
And when I suggested to the Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs that we should delete the clause changing quarterly remittances, even Conservative Members agreed, Mr. Speaker. We had deleted that clause, Mr. Speaker. But officials went to see them one by one at dinner time and the Government Members said no, it's not possible! Just like the Minister of State (Finance) said all evening ... It costs $20 million so we cannot accept it! Civil servants calculated it would cost $20 millions in interests. Since we could not afford that, the Conservative Members came back at the end of the evening, and voted conclusively to finally reintroduce this clause . . . For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am standing here tonight to propose again the same amendment. We simply cannot do this to our senior citizens. If the Government want to put an end to their working capital problem, they should look elsewhere for a solution, not at our senior citizens and our low income people. This is ridiculous, Mr. Speaker, fifteen days! They have enough trouble as it is simply to reconcile their quarterly remittance.
Mr. Speaker, tonight, throughout this debate on tax reform, we have clearly seen the Government's hypocrisy. They want us, and all the population, to believe that they are reducing the deficit, which is not true, and all that time they are taking money from people who really need it. That is why I move to delete this clause, and I hope the House will support my amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make one last attempt to convince the Government of the validity of removing Clause 137 from the Bill. I draw this to the attention of the Deputy Government House Leader (Mr. Lewis).

He is an accountant. He should understand.
