Yes, he is an accountant so he should know how to count.
He is a lawyer, too.

No one should have to apologize for being a lawyer. We do not hold that against the Minister, as you would appreciate, Mr. Speaker.
I want the Deputy Government House Leader to pay attention, because we will ask questions later. The parliamentary committee discussed this Bill in its usual objective fashion. All the committee members reviewed Clause 137, when suddenly one Member, then another and finally all members of the committee agreed that Clause 137 should be removed because it was unfair.
The issue was put to a vote and the committee decided to remove Clause 137. The Assistant Deputy Minister who was in attendance got quite upset and banged on the table so hard that the hub caps nearly flew off the Minister's limousine.
During the dinner hour the Assistant Deputy Minister had time to lobby the individual Conservative members of the committee. After having feasted on the meal, the Conservative Members suddenly had a change of heart and reinstated the clause which they had removed before the dinner hour. When the Conservative members were hungry they were willing to remove Clause 137 because they recognized that it was unfair. After they had feasted, however, they returned to their old Tory selves and reinstated the clause in question which would make senior citizens and many others who have to remit on a quarterly basis do so 15 days before the end of the month.
Apart from everything else, this is mathematically incorrect. How can one talk about quarterly remittance when someone has to remit at a period which has nothing to do with a quarter of the year? If one remits in the last half of the month of the quarter, it is not quarterly, it is something quite different. It is a Tory quarterly period, as my colleague says.
I will let the Conservatives figure out the fraction. It strikes me that it is something quite different from a quarter.
The Government wants to advance the payment by 15 days in order to get an extra bite out of the taxpayers before the end of the tax year. As my colleague said so eloquently, this is exactly what the Government did with the corporate sector. It is now imposing it on individual Canadians.
Conservative Members and all members of the committee recognized this and removed that section because it was unfair. However, as I said, after the Assistant Deputy Minister became really angry, we saw who the real boss is. It was obviously not the Conservative Members because they were whipped into line after having feasted and they came back and reinstated the offensive clause. If there are any Tory Members who have not feasted tonight and are still hungry, I say to them, let them go back to the good selves they were the day their hunger for votes made them withdraw that clause. Why do they not do the same thing now? If it was right then, surely, it must be the right thing to do now.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak on the proposal made by my colleague from Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano). The goal of this motion is to eliminate the change that has been made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his fiscal reform concerning the remittance of tax instalments that must be made quarterly by self-employed workers and that must now be made at an earlier date than before.
Mr. Speaker, that measure in itself is inconceivable, but on top of that, it is being concealed in another way by postponing its implementation until after the election. They forgot to ... I do not know why, Mr. Speaker . ..
Coincidence!

... a coincidence that must ... 1 do not know exactly how it is that we have a fiscal reform that is coming into force on January 1, for the most part except that Clause 137 of the fiscal reform concerning earlier remittance of tax instalments by self-employed workers is now being postponed until fiscal year 1990.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, if that measure had been implemented openly as of today, self-employed workers and especially senior citizens would have been so offended by this petty trick from the Conservatives that they decided not to take any chance and to postpone the whole thing until after the election, just as they did for sales tax reform.
Mr. Speaker, do you know how much this represents in a given year, when it is finally done? It is as if the Government had received $1.1 billion more in revenue during the year when it is implemented.

There is $1.1 billion more for the Canadian Government for only one year. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, in that year, the Tory Government could say it has diminished the deficit by $1.1 billion, but, in fact, that will not be the case, as it has not been the case when the Government changed the remittance day for the personal income tax. It was not the case when the Government changed the remittance date for the sales tax. That was a trick the federal Tory Government used to try to tell the Canadian people that its deficit was lower and so it was able to tell a few stories about it.

Mr. Speaker, when one considers the three measures taken by the Federal Government in the past few years, one can understand why it was able to boast about artificial lowerings of the deficit. This time around, they did not take the risk of doing it right in the middle of an election year. It will be done only in 1990 because given was is going on now a days, sure enough, there will not be any election in 1988, but rather in 1989. That is the last chance, so they said "Let's do it in 1990!". No problem, they said, let's hit them right now and they will make their remittance at this time.

Clearly, they will not be in Government then, but the ones who will still be in Opposition might have the gall to blame the Liberals for it.
Mr. Speaker, I am saying that senior citizens are the ones most severely hit, because people with an income from employment or from a business, whether they are lawyers, accountants or something else, will not have any problems as their money is coming in on a regular basis-daily, weekly or monthly-and moving up the date of remittance of their taxes to the federal Government will not be as critical. However, senior citizens on fixed income, either pension income, paid at the end of the month, or interest income, paid maybe every six months or even annually in the case of Canada Saving Bonds, might have to pay taxes four times a year on an income paid on given dates.
The Government, whether it is Red or Blue, cannot take into account all types of income, but changing the date of remittance from the end to the middle of the month is a hassle for everyone. If the Government gets a billion more that way, it means that someone is not getting the interest on that money, and that someone is the taxpayer. This is a devious way for the Conservative Government to show that in this one year the deficit has been reduced by 1100 million, but it is a one year shot. With the transfer of interest income from senior citizens or self-employed persons to the federal Governement, when the interest rate is said to be around 10 per cent to 15 per cent, depending on the way it is computed and on the frequency of the interest payments, the Government, according to our figures, stand to gain about $20 million from our senior citizens.
The Government tried to de-index old age pensions. Fortunately, that did not work. Now it is making up for that by forcing senior citizens, whose pension or interest income totals $18,000, $20,000, $21,000, to make their remittances on the 15th of the month. Mr. Speaker, this is so unacceptable that even the Conservative Members who sit on the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs decided to vote against it. I hope that, after thinking it over, all Members of the House will see that the members of the committee were right the first time and that this motion moved by my colleague from Saint-Leonard-Anjou (M. Gagliano) should be voted on and agreed to very quickly by the House.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. I think this is one of the silliest and pettiest aspects of the tax reform package the Government has put before the country. This is an absolutely outlandish kind of suggestion. What the Government is asking for is that all those
people who make their income tax payments on a quarterly basis, retired people, small businesses, contractors and some farmers, a whole host of people who pay their taxes on a quarterly basis, will have to change their bookkeeping practices so they can make their cheques out 15 days sooner.
Why is the Government asking that all this disruption take place? It is simply that in the year that it comes into effect, for that one quarter, the Government will have one more bit of money allocated to the previous fiscal year instead of to the next year. For that one year, when it comes into effect, the deficit will be that much smaller by the amount of that particular quarterly payment. That is a pretty silly and cynical reason for forcing people all across the country to change their bookkeeping and accounting practices. I think the fact this may turn out to come into effect during an election year makes people even more cynical and quizzical about the utilization of this particular tax reform package. This is silly and petty and has no place in a genuine tax reform package.
